items.title: SAP Service Cloud Version 2: The Next-Generation Customer Service Platform
items.author: Pranali_Dhange1
items.text:
Customer expectations have changed dramatically. They expect faster resolutions, personalized support, seamless communication across channels, and proactive service experiences. To address these growing demands, SAP has introduced SAP Service Cloud Version 2 (V2), a modern, cloud-native customer service platform designed to transform traditional support operations into intelligent, AI-enabled service experiences. 
 For SAP professionals, especially those working in customer service, CRM, utilities, and transformation programs, understanding Service Cloud V2 is becoming increasingly important.

items.title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 4): Calculating the availability bonus in Convergent Invoicing
items.author: Beaucamp99
items.text:
Introduction 
 In the previous chapters of this series, we explored how a Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) meter-to-cash process can be implemented entirely within SAP IS-U, including the calculation of an availability bonus based on the time a vehicle remains connected to the grid during discharging. 
 In this final chapter, I would like to explore an alternative approach: leveraging SAP Convergent Invoicing (CI) to calculate the availability bonus while keeping the conventional IS-U metering and billing setup unchanged. Instead of introducing additional configurations in IS-U to register meter-reading results in minutes (MIN), we can use CI to calculate the availability bonus based on the number of hours for which the vehicle was connected to the grid. 
 Meanwhile, the charging and discharging quantities continue to be registered through a conventional bidirectional meter in kilowatt-hours (kWh). 
 In other words, our IS-U installation requires only the conventional bidirectional-meter setup for the Meter-to-Cash process. 
 Bidirectional meter ISU_WALLBOX01 installed in installation 4100000514. 

 MR-results for charging and discharging registered in kWh. 

 Billing document 100000005601 – No amount calculated for availability bonus. 

 The availability bonus will be calculated separately in CI and subsequently integrated into the IS-U invoicing process. But how can we bring these two billing streams together and ensure that the customer receives a single invoice covering both the energy-related charges and the availability bonus? 
 Let's explore the required configuration and processing steps, from creating and rating consumption items in CI to joint invoicing and the resulting FI-CA postings. 

 1. Consumption Item Class (CIC) and Billable Item Class (BIC) creation 
 The first step is to configure a new Consumption Item Class (CIC). As a demonstration for this blog, I created a new CIC named “ ZV2G ”, specifically for the V2G solution. 
 Customizing path : 
 Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Consumption Items >> Consumption Item classes >> Maintain Consumption Item Classes 
 Consumption Item class ZV2G 

 Consumption Item class ZV2G – Interface components. 

 Once the CIC has been created and its interface generated, the system creates a corresponding database table. In this example, the generated table is /1FC/0ZV2G400. 
 Consumption Item class ZV2G generated database table - /1FC/0ZV2G400. 

 This table stores the consumption items belonging to the class, including items created for testing and simulation. After rating, the corresponding rating results can be examined in the relevant records. 
 Examples of entries created after simulation runs. 

 Once the consumption items (CIT) have been rated, the system generates the resulting billable items, which can be processed further in Convergent Invoicing through billing execution. For this scenario, however, I also configured integrated billing, which allows the billing document to be created as part of the rating process in my setup. 
 To support the V2G integration, I created a corresponding Billable Item Class (BIC), also named ZV2G. 
 Customizing path: 
 Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Billable Items >> Billable Item classes >> Maintain Billable Item Classes 
 Billable Item class ZV2G. 

 Billable Item class ZV2G – Database table /1FE/0ZV2G4IT00. 

 Billable Item class ZV2G – interface components. 

 It is important to note that this V2G blog post does not aim to explain every aspect of CIC and BIC configuration. The exact configuration depends on the intended integration scenario, the selected interface components, and the requirements of the implementation. 
 However, for a more detailed introduction to Convergent Invoicing and its integration with Utilities, I highly recommend the blog series by Oleh Korolyk, beginning with his article: 
 SAP Billing and Revenue Innovation Management: commodity and non-commodity services on one (or separate) invoice is no longer a dream 
 The article provides an excellent starting point and contains all the links to all other posts in his series. 
 I highly recommend reading this blog series as well! 
 2. Pricing and Rating Configurations 
 As discussed in the previous chapter , the availability bonus in our example is calculated using a price of −0.24 per hour (HR). 
 To implement this calculation in Convergent invoicing, I configured a pricing procedure for the relevant posting area 8200. This can be done by following the customizing path below: 
 Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Pricing >> Assigning Pricing schemas 

 For this example, I used pricing procedure CI1001 , which is an SD pricing procedure that can be maintained using transaction V/08. A pricing procedure defines the sequence of condition types and calculation steps used to determine the applicable price. 
 Pricing procedures CI1001 with the condition types configured in its steps. 

 For this example, I used condition type PST0 to maintain the price applied when rating the consumption items. The condition record can be maintained using transaction VK11, with the relevant combination of sales organization, distribution channel, customer, material, and price unit, according to the condition type configuration. 
 Price condition within condition type PST0. 

 Configurations of material EXTM – Transaction MM03. 

 Once the SD pricing configuration is complete, we must ensure that the relevant pricing logic is executed when the consumption items are rated. 
 For this purpose, I assigned the function module ‘FKK_BIX_RATING_EVENT_30_SD’ in the program extensions of the newly created rating group RV2G . 
 Customizing path : 
 Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups 

 I then assigned our newly created Consumption Item Class ZV2G to the rating group RV2G : 
 Customizing path : 
 Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Assign Consumption Item Classes to Rating Groups 

 With these settings in place, the consumption items can be rated using the configured pricing logic. 
 The negative price represents the customer credit in this example. The resulting amount must be verified against the actual pricing and posting configuration to ensure that the availability bonus is represented correctly in the subsequent billing and FI-CA documents. 
 3. Provider contract for the availability bonus 
 After completing the required CI configuration, we can create the provider contract for the relevant business partner. For this purpose, I used transaction FP_VT1. 
 The provider contract must contain the relevant account and commercial assignments required by the pricing and rating configuration. In this example, these include the business partner, contract account, company code, sales organization, distribution channel, and material. 
 Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data. 

 The provider contract V2G_AVLB is linked to contract account 200000003200. 
 Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data: Linked to contract account 200000003200. 

 In the account assignment data, the provider contract is linked to sales organization 2510, company code BCMP, and product EXTM. 
 Provider contract V2G_AVLB – Account Assignment: Linked to Sales org. 2510; Company code BCMP and Product EXTM (MM). 

 These assignments allow the consumption items to be associated with the relevant customer account and commercial data used for pricing. 
 4. Creation and Rating of Consumption Items 
 Once the provider contract has been created, we can create a consumption item using transaction FKKBIXCIT_CWB. 
 For this demonstration, I created the consumption item manually and linked it to the provider contract. The following information can then be specified: 
 Consumption date 
 Unit of measurement (UoM) 
 Quantity consumed 
 Consumption item type 
 The unit of measurement (UoM) specified in the consumption item must be compatible with the pricing configuration. Since our availability bonus is calculated per hour, I used HR as the unit of measurement. 
 Consumption Item 2608230005000000600001 

 In this example, we create the consumption items manually. In a production environment, however, consumption items would typically be created automatically from data received from an external application. For example, a charging station provider could supply the connection duration of a vehicle through an integration interface. 
 The interface would need to transform and validate the incoming data before creating the corresponding consumption items in your SAP S/4HANA system. 
 SAP provides APIs for creating consumption items. The exact API to use depends on the interface generated for the consumption item class and the SAP release. For the ZV2G class, the generated interface and its supported usage should be verified before implementation. 
 One option would be the general API ‘ FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API ‘: 
 Function Module FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API in which function ‘FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE’ is called. 

 Alternatively, SAP can generate a class-specific RFC function module for each Consumption Item Class, following the naming convention /1FC/XXX_CIT_CREATE_API. These generated interfaces are adapted to the structure of the corresponding class. 
 For our example, after generating the interfaces for CIC ZV2G, the system created the Function Module ‘ /1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API ’, which is tailored to the structure of CIC ZV2G. 
 Function Module /1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API adapted to the structure of CIC ZV2G. 

 Once the Consumption Item has been created, we can execute rating. 

 After successful rating, the consumption item receives the corresponding rated status: 
 Consumption item 2608230005000000600001 with status “Rated”. 

 In a conventional CI process, rating produces billable items that are subsequently processed during billing. As mentioned before, in my example, the rating group is configured for integrated billing, so the billing document is created as part of the configured rating process. 
 Consequently, there is no need to execute a separate billable-item billing run using transaction FKKBIXBIT_MON for this particular scenario. 
 This behavior depends on the integrated-billing configuration and should not be assumed for every CI implementation: 
 Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups 

 The resulting billing document contains the calculated availability bonus. It also carries the quantity and unit of measurement entered in the consumption item, provided the relevant billing-quantity interface component is selected in the billable item class. 
 Billing document 347 including amount, quantity, and unit of measurement. 

 Billable Item Class ZV2G with interface component “Billing quantity”. 

 This completes the CI calculation of the availability bonus. The next step is to integrate the resulting billing document into the IS-U invoicing process. 
 5. Executing the invoicing run in IS-U 
 We now have two billing documents: 
 An IS-U billing document containing the charging and discharging quantities measured in kWh. 
 A CI billing document containing the availability bonus calculated from the connection duration. 
 The objective is to process both documents through IS-U invoicing so that the resulting customer invoice includes both components. 
 To ensure that both billing documents can be invoiced together, you need to customize the invoicing process in which you can specify the source document categories in the selection control.

items.title: From Forecast to Flow: How Agentic AI Is Closing the Supply Chain Planning to Execution Gap
items.author: pavneetbedi

items.title: SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2:Setting Up Principal Propagation with OAuth2 SAML Bearer Authentication
items.author: Yogananda
items.text:
This is my 350th blog post, and I'm excited to continue sharing insights, experiences, and lessons learned with the community. 
 Introduction 
 When integrating SAP BTP services with SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 or SAP Service Cloud Version 2 or ESM , one of the most common requirements is ensuring that the identity of the logged-in user flows seamlessly from the source BTP application into the target SAP Cloud system. This is known as Principal Propagation . 
 Without principal propagation, every API call would authenticate as a technical/service user — losing all user context, audit trails, and authorization logic that depends on who is actually logged in. With it, the end user's identity is securely carried through, enabling fine-grained access control and meaningful audit logs on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud side. 
 This blog walks you through the complete setup using the OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow — the recommended approach for BTP-to-SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 connectivity. 

 How It Works — The Big Picture 
 User (logged into BTP app)
 │
 ▼
BTP Destination (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion)
 │ ── Generates a SAML assertion carrying the user's identity
 ▼
SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 Token Service
 │ ── Validates the assertion against the trusted certificate
 ▼
Returns an OAuth2 Access Token (scoped to that user)
 │
 ▼
API Call executed as the propagated user The trust between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 is established by registering BTP's X.509 certificate as a trusted issuer inside the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant. 
 Prerequisites 
 Access to your SAP BTP Cockpit (subaccount level) 
 Admin access to your SAP Sales Cloud V2 / Service Cloud V2 tenant 
 Ability to call REST APIs on the tenant (e.g., via Postman, Bruno, or curl) 
 Step 1: Download the BTP Trust Certificate 
 Log in to the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your subaccount. 
 Go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust (top-right area of the Destinations page). 
 A .pem certificate file will be downloaded. 
 Open the file and copy only the certificate content — the block between (but not including) the header and footer lines: 

 -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIEXzCCA0... ← copy everything between these lines
-----END CERTIFICATE----- 
 Keep this certificate value handy — you'll need it in the next step. 
 Step 2: Configure Inbound OAuth2 Trust in SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 
 SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 needs to know about BTP as a trusted SAML assertion issuer. This is done via a dedicated IAM Service REST API on your tenant. 
 Important restriction: Only one OAuth2 SAML Bearer Inbound Configuration can exist per tenant. 
 2a. Check if a Configuration Already Exists 
 Send a GET request to check the current state: 
 GET <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration 
 If a configuration exists with the same BTP certificate → you can reuse it as-is. 
 If a configuration exists with a different certificate → update it (Step 2b). 
 If no configuration exists → create a new one (Step 2c). 
 2b. Update an Existing Configuration (PUT) 
 PUT <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration/<id>
Content-Type: application/json

{
 "id": "<existing Id found in Step 2a>",
 "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
 "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
} 
 2c. Create a New Configuration (POST) 
 POST <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
Content-Type: application/json

{
 "id": "<BTP Subaccount UUID (This is to easily identify or you can provide your own UUID v4 format>",
 "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
 "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
} 
 2d. Save the Response Values 
 A successful POST or PUT returns a JSON response like this: 
 {
 "value": {
 "id": "...",
 "grantType": "SAML2_BEARER",
 "nameIdType": "EMAIL",
 "spEntityId": "...",
 "audience": "<AUDIENCE>",
 "tokenServiceUrl": "<TOKEN_URL>",
 "clientId": "<CLIENT_ID>",
 "scopes": ["<SCOPE_ID>"],
 "clientAppName": "...",
 "certificate": "..."
 }
} 
 Note down these four values — you'll need them in Step 3: 
 Field Used As 
 audience Audience in BTP destination 
 tokenServiceUrl Token Service URL in BTP destination 
 clientId → appears as CLIENT_ID Client Key in BTP destination 
 scopes[0] → SCOPE_ID Scope in BTP destination 
 Step 3: Create the BTP Destination 
 Now configure a destination in your BTP subaccount that uses the inbound configuration values you just collected. 
 Go to SAP BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations → New Destination . 
 Fill in the following fields: 
 Property Value 
 Name Your choice (e.g., SalesCloudV2_PrincipalProp ) 
 Type HTTP 
 URL <Your SAP Sales/Service Cloud Tenant Host URL> 
 Authentication OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion 
 Audience <AUDIENCE> from the inbound config response 
 AuthnContextClassRef urn:none 
 Client Key <CLIENT_ID> from the inbound config response 
 Token Service URL <TOKEN_URL> from the inbound config response 
 Scope <SCOPE_ID> from the inbound config response 
 nameIdFormat urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress 
 The nameIdFormat value tells the system to use the user's email address as the SAML NameID — this is how the user identity is matched on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 or ESM side. 

 Step 4: Configure Trusted Domains in SAP BTP Authorization & Trust Management 
 As a final step, ensure that your SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant domain is registered as a trusted domain in SAP BTP's Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA/SAP Cloud Identity Services). 
 Refer to the official SAP documentation: Configure Trusted Domains for SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service . 
 This ensures that SAML assertions issued by BTP are only accepted by explicitly trusted target systems — an important security boundary. 

 Summary 
 Here's a quick recap of the end-to-end setup: 
 Step 1 → Download BTP X.509 Trust Certificate
Step 2 → Register certificate as Inbound OAuth2 Config on SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2
Step 3 → Create OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion Destination in BTP using response values
Step 4 → Register SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 domain as trusted in BTP Auth & Trust 
 Once complete, any BTP application or service using this destination will automatically propagate the logged-in user's identity to SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 — without requiring users to re-authenticate or sharing technical credentials. 
 Key Takeaways 
 Principal Propagation bridges the identity gap between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2, preserving the real user context across systems. 
 The trust is certificate-based — BTP's signing certificate is registered directly in the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 IAM service. 
 The fixed UUID ( 34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667 ) is a well-known system identifier for this configuration — don't change it. 
 Only one inbound configuration is allowed per tenant, so manage it carefully across teams. 
 User matching relies on email address as the SAML NameID — ensure users exist with the same email in both systems. 
 Share to your colleagues or Have questions or ran into issues during the setup? Drop them in the comments below.

items.title: SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM: Navigate Your SAP Universe with Product Switch
items.author: Yogananda
items.text:
The Problem Nobody Talks About 
 You're in the middle of a customer interaction in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 or ESM , and you need to quickly jump to SAP Engagement Cloud for Promotions , check something in S/4HANA , or pull up an Analytics Cloud report. What do you do? 
 Most users open a new browser tab, hunt for the bookmark, type in a URL, and wait for a login screen — only to realize they've already lost 90 seconds and their customer's attention. 
 There's a better way. And it's already built into the platform you're using. 
 What is the Product Switch inside your SAP Applications? 
 The Product Switch is a UI5 Shell Bar component — the ⋮⋮⋮ (grid) icon sitting at the top-right corner of your SAP application shell. A single click opens a product launchpad popover showing all the SAP applications available to your organization, arranged in a clean icon grid. 
 Think of it as your personal SAP application launcher — contextual, fast, and always one click away. 
 As shown in the UI5 Demo Kit sample ( sap.f.ShellBarProductSwitch ), the popover can surface: 
 The active application is highlighted (see Home with its blue border in the screenshot), so users always know where they are. 
 Why This Matters in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM 
 SAP's Enterprise Service Management (ESM) consolidates cross-functional service workflows — field service, IT helpdesk, HR service, and customer service — under one umbrella, often running alongside Sales Cloud v2. This means your users are citizen travellers across multiple SAP applications throughout their workday. 
 Without a unified launcher, context-switching becomes friction. With Product Switch integrated into the Sales & Service Cloud v2 shell, it becomes seamless. 
 The SSO Advantage: One Login, All Applications 
 This is the standout benefit. Because SAP's cloud portfolio uses SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS) for federated SSO, the moment you authenticate into Sales & ServiceCloud v2 or ESM, that identity token is valid across all connected SAP applications in your landscape. 
 When you click an application tile in the Product Switch: 
 The target application receives your existing session token. 
 No login prompt appears. 
 You land directly on the application home page — in seconds . 
 No re-authentication. No password prompts. No lost context. 
 This is especially powerful for: 
 Sales reps who pivot between Sales Cloud v2, Analytics Cloud dashboards, Side-by-Side Extensions, Emersys, Engagement Cloud, S4 HANA Public Cloud and CPQ. 
 Service agents who navigate between ESM tickets, S/4HANA inventory checks, and Field Service Management via Agent Desktop or from CTI(Computer telephony Interaction). 
 Managers who review CRM pipeline data and then jump to finance or workforce analytics. 
 How to Pin Your Applications: Personalization at Its Best 
 The Product Switch is not just a static list — it supports any of your SAP Applications to easily launch. Users can simply navigate in smoother way without any login screen(with SSO enabled): 
 Your SAP Sales & Service Cloud or ESM Admin need to perform this below ###
---- Sample ---

POST {{url}}/sap/c4c/api/v1/extensibility-service/externalAppMenuItems
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer {{accessToken}}

{ 
 "name": "appGyver", 
 "label": "App Gyver", 
 "url": "https://platform.appgyver.black/c4c/launch", 
 "iconUrl": "https://platform.appgyver.eu/favicon.png" 
} 
 How to Access the Product Switch in Sales & Service Cloud v2 or ESM 
 Log in to your SAP Sales Cloud v2 or ESM tenant. 
 Look for the ⋮⋮⋮ grid icon in the top-right corner of the Shell Bar (next to your user avatar and notifications bell). 
 Click the icon — the Product Switch popover opens. 
 Click any application tile to navigate instantly, leveraging your active SSO session. 

 Business Value Summary 
 Benefit Impact 
 One-click navigation Reduces app-switching time from ~90s to ~3s 
 SSO-powered, zero re-login Eliminates authentication friction across all connected apps 
 Personalized pinning Users organize apps to match their workflow 
 Admin-governed catalog IT controls which apps surface — aligned with licensing and roles 
 Native UI5 component No custom development needed; works out of the box in v2 shell 
 Closing Thought 
 The Product Switch is one of those features that seems small until you use it every day. For organizations running SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 alongside ESM, SAP Engagement Cloud , SAP Emersys, S/4HANA, Analytics Cloud, Side-by-Side Extensions or any custom developed applications or any other SAP cloud product — it is the connective tissue that turns a portfolio of applications into a unified work experience. 
 One shell. One login. Your entire SAP landscape, one click away.

items.title: Generating Adobe Form PDF Using Custom Entity and Query Provider Class in SAP RAP
items.author: Mohan-Raj-M
items.text:
Generating Adobe Form PDF Using Custom Entity and Query Provider Class in SAP RAP 
 Why I built this 
 A few months ago our finance team came to me with a simple-sounding request: [a downstream approval portal / external system] needed to show the Journal Voucher printout for a posted accounting document — the same PDF users print from the Manage Journal Entries app. 
 Until then the process was manual. Someone opened the document in SAP, printed the voucher to PDF, and uploaded or emailed it. With [X] vouchers a day, that was slow and error-prone, and the attachment often did not match the final posted version. 
 We had three constraints: 
 The PDF had to come from the existing Adobe Form template , so the layout stayed exactly as finance had approved it. 
 Nothing should be stored. The voucher must always reflect the current document, not a copy saved days earlier. 
 The consumer was [CPI / a UI5 app / both] , so the output had to be a plain OData service. 
 My first instinct was a classic Gateway service with GET_STREAM . But we were building the rest of the extension in RAP, and I wanted one consistent model. A custom entity with a query provider class turned out to be the cleanest fit. This blog walks through what I built, and a few things I would do differently. 
 Where this applies 
 I built and tested this on [SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2408 / S/4HANA 2023 on-premise — confirm] . 
 The approach depends on three things: 
 Output Management form templates. The ZZ1_ prefix means the template was created as a custom form in the Maintain Form Templates app (key-user extensibility). Classic SFP forms called through FP_JOB_OPEN follow a different path. 
 CL_SOMU_FORM_SERVICES must be available and usable from your development language version. Check its release state in your system before you design around it. 
 Adobe Document Services (ADS) must be configured — on cloud via SAP Forms service by Adobe, on-premise via your ADS connection. 
 If you are on an older on-premise release without RAP custom entities, the same idea works with a SEGW service and GET_STREAM . 
 How it works 
 The request flows through five layers, and the PDF is never persisted: 
 A Fiori app or API call hits the OData service with Company Code, Fiscal Year and Accounting Document. 
 The custom CDS entity ZFI_C_JV_PDF receives the parameters. 
 The query provider class ZFI_CL_JV_PDF reads them and calls CL_SOMU_FORM_SERVICES . 
 The Journal Voucher template ZZ1_FI_JOURNAL_VOUCHER renders the PDF as an XSTRING . 
 The class converts it to Base64 and returns it in the OData response. 
 Step 1: Custom CDS entity 
 The entity takes the three document keys as parameters and exposes one field for the PDF. 
 @EndUserText.label: 'Journal Voucher Form : PDF Extractor'
@ObjectModel.query.implementedBy: 'ABAP:ZFI_CL_JV_PDF'
define custom entity ZFI_C_JV_PDF
 with parameters
 @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ entity: { name: 'I_CompanyCodeStdVH', element: 'CompanyCode' } }]
 P_COMPANYCODE : bukrs,
 P_FISCALYEAR : gjahr,
 @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ entity: { name: 'I_AccountingDocumentStdVH', element: 'AccountingDocument' } }]
 P_ACCDOC : belnr_d
{
 key pdf : abap.string(0);
} 
 @ObjectModel.query.implementedBy points the entity to the ABAP class. The value helps on the parameters made testing in the Fiori preview much easier. 
 Step 2: Query provider class 
 CLASS zfi_cl_jv_pdf DEFINITION PUBLIC FINAL CREATE PUBLIC.
 PUBLIC SECTION.
 INTERFACES if_rap_query_provider.
ENDCLASS. 
 Step 3: Query logic 
 This is the version I ended up with after testing. Compared with my first draft, it reads the paging object, only sets the count when it is requested, and does not return an empty Base64 string when the form fails. 
 CLASS zfi_cl_jv_pdf IMPLEMENTATION.

 METHOD if_rap_query_provider~select.

 DATA: lt_result TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF zfi_c_jv_pdf,
 lv_content TYPE xstring,
 lt_keys TYPE cl_somu_form_services=>ty_gt_key.

 IF io_request->is_data_requested( ) = abap_false.
 RETURN.
 ENDIF.

 " The framework expects paging to be read, even for a single-row result
 DATA(lo_paging) = io_request->get_paging( ).

 DATA(lt_params) = io_request->get_parameters( ).

 lt_keys = VALUE #(
 ( name = 'CompanyCode' value = VALUE #( lt_params[ parameter_name = 'P_COMPANYCODE' ]-value OPTIONAL ) )
 ( name = 'FiscalYear' value = VALUE #( lt_params[ parameter_name = 'P_FISCALYEAR' ]-value OPTIONAL ) )
 ( name = 'AccountingDocument' value = VALUE #( lt_params[ parameter_name = 'P_ACCDOC' ]-value OPTIONAL ) ) ).

 TRY.
 cl_somu_form_services=>get_instance( )->get_document(
 EXPORTING iv_form_name = 'ZZ1_FI_JOURNAL_VOUCHER'
 it_key = lt_keys
 IMPORTING ev_content = lv_content ).
 CATCH cx_somu_error INTO DATA(lx_form).
 " Log lx_form->get_text( ) to your application log here
 CLEAR lv_content.
 ENDTRY.

 IF lv_content IS NOT INITIAL.
 lt_result = VALUE #( ( pdf = cl_web_http_utility=>encode_x_base64( lv_content ) ) ).
 ENDIF.

 IF io_request->is_total_numb_of_rec_requested( ).
 io_response->set_total_number_of_records( lines( lt_result ) ).
 ENDIF.
 io_response->set_data( lt_result ).

 ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS. 
 Step 4: Adobe Form generation 
 The core call is GET_DOCUMENT on the form service. It takes the template name and the keys, and returns the rendered PDF. 
 cl_somu_form_services=>get_instance( )->get_document(
 EXPORTING iv_form_name = 'ZZ1_FI_JOURNAL_VOUCHER'
 it_key = lt_keys
 IMPORTING ev_content = lv_content ). 
 Component Description 
 Form name The Adobe Form template from Maintain Form Templates 
 Keys Parameters passed to the form's data source 
 Output PDF in XSTRING format 
 Step 5: Convert the PDF to Base64 
 The entity's pdf field is a string, so the binary XSTRING is encoded before it goes into the response. 
 DATA(lv_pdf) = cl_web_http_utility=>encode_x_base64( lv_content ). 
 The consumer decodes it to display or download the PDF. The reasoning behind this choice is in the section on Base64 vs media resources below. 
 Step 6: Return the data in the RAP response 
 The Base64 string goes into the result table, and the framework turns it into the OData response. 
 lt_result = VALUE #( ( pdf = lv_pdf ) ).

IF io_request->is_total_numb_of_rec_requested( ).
 io_response->set_total_number_of_records( lines( lt_result ) ).
ENDIF.
io_response->set_data( lt_result ). 
 Step 7: Expose and test 
 Create a service definition exposing ZFI_C_JV_PDF , bind it as OData V4 (UI or Web API), and test with: 
 /ZFI_C_JV_PDF(P_COMPANYCODE='1000',P_FISCALYEAR='2026',P_ACCDOC='0100000012')/Set 
 The response looks like this: 
 {
 "value": [
 { "pdf": "JVBERi0xLjQKJeLjz9MKMSAwIG9iago..." }
 ]
} 
 A quick sanity check: a valid PDF in Base64 always starts with JVBERi (the encoding of %PDF- ). If you see anything else, the form returned an error page or nothing at all. 
 Why Base64 instead of a media resource 
 This was the design decision I spent the most time on. RAP does support binary content as a media resource, using @Semantics.largeObject on a rawstring field with a MIME type. So why return a Base64 string? 
 Nothing to persist. Large-object handling fits best when the binary lives on a BO, usually in a table. My PDF is generated on every call, so there is no stored record to stream from. 
 The custom entity stays simple. A single string field in a JSON response needs no extra annotations, MIME-type field or stream handling. 
 The consumer wanted JSON. [CPI] reads the field, decodes it with a standard step, and passes it on. A UI5 app can decode it with atob() and open it in a PDF viewer. No special $value handling is needed. 
 The trade-off is real, though: 
 Aspect Base64 in JSON Media resource (largeObject) 
 Payload size About 33% larger than the PDF Raw binary, no overhead 
 Fiori Elements Needs custom decode logic Built-in download / open 
 Best for Small to medium documents, integrations Large files, stored attachments 
 Our vouchers are [50–300 KB] , so the overhead did not matter. For multi-MB documents, or a Fiori Elements app with a native download button, I would choose a media resource on a managed BO instead. 
 Advantages of this approach 
 Fits the RAP model, with no separate SEGW service 
 No PDF stored in the database; every call reflects the current document 
 Reuses the existing, approved Adobe Form layout 
 Easy to consume from Fiori apps and CPI integrations 
 What I learned along the way 
 Empty CATCH blocks hide everything. My first version swallowed cx_somu_error . When a document number was wrong, the service happily returned an empty Base64 string, and it took me a while to see why. Log the exception text, or return no rows. 
 Key names must match the form's data source exactly. CompanyCode , FiscalYear and AccountingDocument are the key names the form template expects. A typo raises no syntax error, only an empty or failed form. 
 Read the paging object. Even with one row, the framework can complain if $top or $skip is sent and the provider never calls get_paging( ) . 
 Keep the query provider thin. All the data selection lives in the form's data source. The class only passes keys and converts the output, which kept response times around [1–2 seconds] per voucher. 
 Conclusion 
 What started as a request to stop printing vouchers by hand became a reusable pattern. The same class now works for [other forms, e.g. payment advice] by changing only the form name and keys. 
 If you have a template in Maintain Form Templates and need its PDF in an API or Fiori app, a custom entity with a query provider is a quick, clean way to get there. I'd like to hear how others handled larger documents — did you go with media resources, or something else?

items.author: AhsanSyed
items.text:
Hello finance experts! I’m excited to walk you through the latest finance innovations introduced in our 2608 release. This update is loaded with capabilities that add more intelligence, automation, and visibility to your finance operations. We’re continuing our mission to streamline core activities, elevate analytical depth, and enable quicker, data-driven decisions. Want the short version of the top Finance highlights in 2608? Watch my quick video. For a complete rundown of everything included in this release, take a look at the table of contents below. Let’s jump into the highlights! Video 1. Release Highlight Video for Finance in SAP Cloud ERP 2608

 SAP Fiori app for posting asset transfers

 Revenue Management

 Managing Direct Debit Prenotifications in Contract Accounting 
 Display of General Ledger Items in Contract Accounting (Demo video) 
 Accounting & Financial Close 
 End-to-end cost settlement process (CLM) 
 The latest 2608 release of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition introduces a range of powerful capabilities, including the new End-to-end cost settlement process within the Finance capability area. While the provided reference document lists this as a key innovation, it does not contain a detailed description of its specific functionalities. However, based on standard SAP principles and the direction of financial innovations, we can explore what such a process entails and the value it delivers to your organization. 

 An end-to-end cost settlement process is a critical function for maintaining financial accuracy and transparency. In essence, it governs the complete lifecycle of how costs are collected and allocated throughout the organization. This process involves capturing costs from various sources such as internal orders, projects, or cost centers where expenses are initially incurred and systematically settling them to their final destination cost objects, like a fixed asset, a profitability segment, or another department. A robust, integrated process ensures that all expenditures are accounted for correctly, providing a true and fair view of costs for specific activities, products, or services. 

 The primary benefit of implementing a comprehensive cost settlement process is the significant improvement in financial control and operational efficiency. By automating the periodic allocation of costs, businesses can drastically reduce the manual effort required during period-end closing, which in turn minimizes the risk of human error and accelerates the closing cycle. This automation leads to greater transparency, as it provides a clear and auditable trail of how costs flow through the enterprise. Ultimately, this empowers management with more accurate and timely data for crucial activities such as profitability analysis, budget monitoring, and informed strategic decision-making. 
 Introduction of configurable depreciation profiles 
 In essence, this feature provides organizations with greater control and flexibility over how they calculate and manage the depreciation of their fixed assets. Instead of being limited to standard, predefined depreciation methods, finance professionals can now define and customize their own depreciation calculation rules directly within the system to meet specific business or regulatory needs. 

 The primary benefit of this new capability is the enhanced flexibility it offers for global and local compliance. Many businesses operate in jurisdictions with unique statutory requirements for asset valuation that may not be covered by standard depreciation keys. Configurable depreciation profiles empower users to create tailored calculation methods that precisely align with these local accounting principles, reducing the need for manual workarounds and complex spreadsheets outside the ERP system. Consequently, this leads to more accurate and compliant financial reporting, improves the efficiency of period-end closing activities, and ensures that asset values are reflected correctly on the balance sheet, thereby strengthening financial governance and transparency across the enterprise. 
 SAP Fiori app for posting asset transfers 
 As part of our commitment to enhancing core financial processes, SAP has introduced a new SAP Fiori app specifically for posting asset transfers. This application provides a modern, user-friendly interface dedicated to managing the movement of fixed assets within your organization. In simple terms, this tool is designed to streamline the process of executing various transfer scenarios, such as moving an asset from one company code to another or reclassifying an asset. By leveraging the intuitive SAP Fiori user experience, this app simplifies a critical function within asset accounting. 

 The introduction of this dedicated Fiori application delivers significant benefits to finance professionals. The primary advantage is a marked improvement in user efficiency and process transparency. The app offers a guided, intuitive workflow that reduces the manual effort and complexity traditionally associated with asset transfers. This simplification helps minimize the risk of data entry errors and accelerates tasks related to asset portfolio management. Consequently, organizations can achieve a more agile and controlled approach to asset accounting, ensuring that asset data remains accurate and compliant across the enterprise. 
 Central Task Model management 
 This new feature provides a unified and simplified approach to managing your financial closing tasks. Essentially, Central Task Model management allows users to create, edit, publish, and delete task models directly within the SAP Advanced Financial Closing interface. Previously, this process required switching to a separate communication system. Now, the entire lifecycle of task models, including the maintenance of task model types and job variants, is consolidated into a single, intuitive environment. Once a task model is published, it becomes immediately available for use in your task list templates, facilitating the swift creation and reuse of standardized closing activities. 

 The primary benefit of this centralized approach is a marked increase in operational efficiency for both IT and business users. By eliminating the need to navigate between different systems, we significantly reduce the manual effort and time required to manage closing tasks. This streamlined workflow allows for the faster creation and deployment of reusable task definitions, making your financial close process more agile and responsive. Furthermore, the feature introduces a dedicated change log, which offers complete transparency and auditability by tracking all modifications made to task models and their related objects. This enhances governance and control, ensuring your financial closing activities are both efficient and compliant. 
 Journal Entry Agent 
 The Journal Entry Agent is a powerful new tool designed to fundamentally automate and simplify the creation of journal entries within SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. In essence, it acts as an intelligent assistant that processes spreadsheet data to generate accurate and compliant financial postings. Users can initiate this process conversationally by submitting data files through our digital assistant, Joule. The agent then analyzes the spreadsheet's content, automatically maps the columns to the required journal entry fields, and produces structured proposals. These proposals are then made available for finance professionals to review, adjust if necessary, and post via the dedicated Manage Journal Entry Proposals application. 

 Image 01. Journal Entry Agent 
 The primary benefit of utilizing the Journal Entry Agent is a significant increase in operational efficiency and accuracy. By automating what is often a time-consuming and manual task, the agent drastically reduces the time spent on data entry, allowing your finance team to focus on more strategic, value-added activities. This automation also improves the accuracy of journal entries, minimizing the risk of errors. Furthermore, the feature enhances transparency, as each generated proposal is directly linked to its source file, ensuring a clear and auditable trail. Ultimately, these capabilities streamline the entire journal entry workflow, contributing to a faster and more efficient period-end closing process for your organization. 
 Financial Planning & Analysis 
 Comprehensive analytical capabilities for material values in actual costing 
 The recent 2608 release of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition introduces a significant advancement within the Finance portfolio: Comprehensive analytical capabilities for material values in actual costing. In simple terms, actual costing is a method used to determine the true cost of materials after a period has ended by incorporating variances, such as those from purchase prices or resource consumption. While this provides a highly accurate financial picture, analyzing the vast amount of resulting data can be complex. This new feature directly addresses that challenge by providing powerful, embedded tools to dissect and understand the detailed components of your material costs with greater ease and clarity. 

 Video 2.Comprehensive analytical capabilities for material values in actual costing 
 The primary benefit of this enhancement is the profound level of transparency it offers to financial controllers and cost accountants. By leveraging these new analytical capabilities, users can move beyond high-level summaries to perform deep-dive analyses into cost drivers and variances. This facilitates more accurate profitability analysis, empowers more informed make-or-buy decisions, and helps identify opportunities for cost optimization within the supply chain. Ultimately, this leads to a more streamlined and insightful period-end closing process, reducing manual effort and enabling your finance teams to become strategic partners to the business by providing actionable intelligence derived directly from your actual material values. 
 AI-assisted error resolution for cost accounting 
 As part of the recent 2608 release for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, we are excited to introduce a suite of intelligent capabilities. Among these is the new AI-assisted error resolution for cost accounting. This feature is designed to fundamentally simplify and accelerate how finance professionals handle discrepancies within their cost accounting processes. In essence, it leverages the power of artificial intelligence to proactively identify, analyze, and guide users in resolving errors that can occur during critical tasks like cost allocations, internal settlements, and other period-end closing activities. By intelligently diagnosing the root cause of an issue, the system can reduce the need for extensive manual investigation, empowering users to address problems more efficiently.

items.title: Building a RAP Managed Business Object on SAP BTP — A Complete Step-by-Step Guide
items.author: iamnaveen
items.text:
SAP RAP Managed Scenario — Step-by-Step Guide 
 A complete, beginner-friendly implementation of an SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) Managed Business Object — built on SAP BTP ABAP Environment Trial. This repository walks through every layer of the RAP stack from database tables to the Fiori Elements UI, with detailed explanations of why each artifact exists, not just how to create it. 
 Table of Contents 
 Overview 
 Architecture 
 Prerequisites 
 Step 1 — Database Table 
 Step 2 — Draft Table 
 Step 3 — Interface View (Z*_I) 
 Step 4 — Consumption View (Z*_C) 
 Step 5 — Metadata Extension 
 Step 6 — Behavior Definition (Interface) 
 Step 7 — Behavior Definition (Projection) 
 Step 8 — Behavior Implementation 
 Step 9 — Service Definition & Binding 
 Key Takeaways 
 Overview What is RAP? The ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) is SAP's modern, cloud-ready framework for building transactional Fiori applications in ABAP Cloud. It replaces older approaches like BOPF and classic ABAP MVC, and is the standard for SAP S/4HANA Cloud and BTP ABAP Environment development. RAP provides: 
 A structured, layered architecture from database to UI 
 Built-in OData service generation (no manual SEGW needed) 
 Framework-managed CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) 
 Draft handling for save/resume workflows 
 Clean Core compliance — no modifications to SAP standard objects 
 What is the Managed Scenario? 
 Type Who handles CRUD? When to use 
 Managed RAP Framework automatically New custom BOs — no legacy dependencies 
 Unmanaged Developer writes all logic Wrapping legacy function modules / BAPIs 
 In the Managed scenario , the RAP framework automatically handles database INSERT , UPDATE , DELETE , and SELECT operations. You only write code for custom business logic like validations, determinations, and custom actions. This makes it the fastest and cleanest way to build a new Business Object from scratch. 
 Architecture 
 The RAP stack follows a strict layered architecture. Each layer has a specific responsibility, and no layer should skip or bypass another. 
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ 
 │ Fiori Elements UI │ 
 │ (Auto-generated from OData) │ 
 └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘ 
 │ OData V4 
 ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐ 
 │ Service Definition + Service Binding │ 
 │ (Exposes which entities go into OData) │ 
 └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘ 
 │ 
 ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐ 
 │ PROJECTION LAYER (ZC_*) │ 
 │ CDS Consumption View + Projection Behavior Def. │ 
 │ (Service-specific: UI annotations, field exposure) │ 
 └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘ 
 │ as projection on 
 ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐ 
 │ INTERFACE LAYER (ZR_* / ZI_*) │ 
 │ CDS Interface View + Base Behavior Definition │ 
 │ (Service-agnostic: data model, business logic) │ 
 └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘ 
 │ 
 ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐ 
 │ DATABASE LAYER │ 
 │ Main Table (ZDB_*) + Draft Table (*_D) │ 
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 
 Prerequisites 
 Before you start, make sure you have: 
 SAP BTP Trial account — 
 Steps to create Trial account 
 ABAP Environment trial instance provisioned on BTP 
 Eclipse IDE with ABAP Development Tools (ADT) plugin installed 
 Connected to your BTP ABAP system via ADT 
 Basic understanding of ABAP syntax and CDS views 
 Step 1 — Database Table (Main Table ) 
 What is it? 
 The database table is the foundation of your Business Object . It is the actual physical table in the SAP HANA database where all your application data is permanently stored. Every field you want to persist — travel ID, agency, customer, price, status — must be defined here first. 
 Why do we create it? 
 Without a database table, there is no place to store data. The entire RAP stack above it — CDS views, behavior definitions, OData services — are all abstractions built on top of this table. The table is the single source of truth for your BO's data. 
 Structure of a RAP-compliant database table 
 A RAP managed table must follow specific conventions: 
 @EndUserText.label : 'Products'
@AbapCatalog.enhancement.category : #NOT_EXTENSIBLE
@AbapCatalog.tableCategory : #TRANSPARENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #A
@AbapCatalog.dataMaintenance : #RESTRICTED
define table znk_t_product {

 key client : abap.clnt not null;
 key pro_uuid : sysuuid_x16 not null;
 key product_id : abap.char(10) not null;
 description : abap.char(40);
 @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure : 'znk_t_product.uom'
 qty : abap.quan(8,3);
 uom : abap.unit(3);
 @Semantics.amount.currencyCode : 'znk_t_product.currency'
 price : abap.curr(15,2);
 currency : abap.cuky;
 mfg_date : abap.datn;
 exp_date : abap.datn;
 validdays : abap.int4;
 plant : abap.char(4);
 local_created_by : abp_creation_user;
 local_created_at : abp_creation_tstmpl;
 local_last_changed_by : abp_locinst_lastchange_user;
 local_last_changed_at : abp_locinst_lastchange_tstmpl;
 last_changed_at : abp_lastchange_tstmpl;

} 
 Important: The last_changed_at field with type abp_lastchange_tstmpl is critical for the ETag mechanism. When two users try to update the same record simultaneously, RAP compares this timestamp to detect conflicts and reject stale updates. 
 Key fields explained 
 Field Type Purpose 
 client abap.clnt SAP client field — mandatory first key in every table 
 product_id Business key Unique identifier for each product record 
 local_created_byy / local_created_at Admin fields Auto-populated by RAP framework — track who created the record 
 local_last_changed_by / local_last_changed_at Admin fields Auto-populated — track last modifier 
 last_changed_at ETag field Used by RAP for optimistic locking / concurrency control 
 Step 2 — Draft Table (Why It Exists) 
 What is a Draft Table? 
 The draft table is a temporary storage table where incomplete, unsaved data is held while a user is still filling in a form. It has an identical structure to your main database table, with some additional draft-specific fields added by the framework. 
 By convention, draft tables are named the same as the main table with a _D suffix: 
 Main table : ZNK_T_PRODUCT ← permanent, saved data
Draft table : ZNK_T_PRODUCT_D ← temporary, in-progress data 
 Why do we need a Draft Table? 
 Imagine a user opens a "Create Product" form in a Fiori app and starts filling in the fields — Plant, UOM, MFG & Exp dates. Halfway through, their browser crashes, or they need to attend a meeting. Without draft handling, all their work is lost. 
 With Draft Handling: 
 User opens form
 │
 ▼
Data saved to DRAFT TABLE immediately (auto-save)
 │
 ├── User continues tomorrow → draft is still there ✅
 ├── User switches device → draft is still there ✅
 └── User clicks "Save" → data moves to MAIN TABLE ✅
 draft record is deleted ✅ 
 The draft table ensures no data loss during long-running create/edit operations. It also enables the "Edit" button behavior in Fiori apps — when you click Edit on a saved record, RAP copies the record to the draft table so your edits don't affect the live data until you explicitly save. 
 How to define the Draft Table 
 You don't write the draft table manually field by field. You reference it in your Behavior Definition and let ADT generate it: 
 -- In your Behavior Definition:
managed implementation in class zbp_nk_product_i unique;
strict ( 2 );
with draft;
define behavior for znk_product_I //alias <alias_name>
persistent table znk_t_product -- ← your main table
draft table znk_t_product_d -- ← your draft table (RAP manages this) 
... 
 When you activate the behavior definition, ADT automatically creates the draft table with the correct structure. 
 Draft Table vs Main Table — Side by Side 
 Aspect Main Table Draft Table 
 Purpose Permanent business data Temporary in-progress data 
 When data lands here On "Save" action On every field change (auto-save) 
 Who can see it All users Only the user editing 
 Deleted when Never (business record) On Save or Discard 
 Named ZNK_T_PRODUCT ZNK_T_PRODUCT_D 
 Created by Developer manually ADT generates from BDEF Step 3 — Interface View (Z*_I) 
 What is the Interface View? 
 The Interface View is the base CDS View Entity that sits directly on top of your database table. It forms the service-agnostic data model of your Business Object — meaning it defines the complete data structure without any UI-specific concerns. 
 By convention, Interface Views are prefixed with ZR_ (R = Root) for root entities or ZI_ (I = Interface). 
 @AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Product Interface View'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define root view entity znk_product_I as select from znk_t_product
association [0..1] to I_Currency as _Currency on $projection.Currency = _Currency.Currency
association [ 0..1] to I_UnitOfMeasure as _Uom on $projection.Uom = _Uom.UnitOfMeasure

{
 key pro_uuid as ProUuid,
 key product_id as ProductId,
 description as Description,
 @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'uom'
 qty as Qty,
 @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ 
 entity.name: 'I_UnitOfMeasure',
 entity.element: 'UnitOfMeasure',
 useForValidation: true
 }]
 uom as Uom,
 @Semantics.amount.currencyCode: 'currency'
 price as Price,
 @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ 
 entity.name: 'I_Currency',
 entity.element: 'Currency',
 useForValidation: true
 }]
 currency as Currency,
 mfg_date as MfgDate,
 exp_date as ExpDate,
 plant as Plant,
 validdays as ValidDays,
 @Semantics.user.createdBy: true
 local_created_by as LocalCreatedBy,
 @Semantics.systemDateTime.createdAt: true
 local_created_at as LocalCreatedAt,
 @Semantics.user.lastChangedBy: true
 local_last_changed_by as LocalLastChangedBy,
 @Semantics.systemDateTime.localInstanceLastChangedAt: true
 local_last_changed_at as LocalLastChangedAt,
 @Semantics.systemDateTime.lastChangedAt: true
 last_changed_at as LastChangedAt,
 _Uom as UomDetails,
 _Currency as CurrencyDetails
 // Make association public
} 
 Why do we need the Interface View? 
 The Interface View serves several critical purposes: 
 1. Abstraction from the database table The database table uses technical field names and types. The Interface View can rename, cast, and join fields into a cleaner business model. If the table structure changes, only the interface view needs to be updated — everything above is unaffected. 
 2. It is the root of the composition tree The keyword define root view entity declares this as the top of a Business Object hierarchy. All child entities (like Booking under Travel) are connected back to this root via COMPOSITION OF associations. 
 3. It is reusable across multiple services The interface view has NO UI annotations, NO Fiori-specific logic. This means the same interface view can power: 
 A Fiori Elements app (via projection view → OData) 
 A remote API (via a different projection) 
 4. Associations are defined here Associations to related entities (Currency, UnitOfMeasure) are defined on the interface view so they are available to all Products. 
 The define root view entity keyword 
 This keyword does two important things: 
 It declares this CDS view as a Root Entity of a Business Object 
 It enables it to have its own Behavior Definition repository object 
 Only root entities can define composition of child associations Step 4 — Consumption View (Z*_C) 
 What is the Consumption View? 
 The Consumption View (also called the Projection View ) sits on top of the Interface View and represents a service-specific, tailored window into the Business Object. It is what gets exposed to the outside world — via OData, via a Fiori app, via an API. 
 By convention, Consumption Views are prefixed or suffixed with ZC_ (C = Consumption). 
 @AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@End

items.title: The Evolution of the SAP User Interface: From SAP GUI to Fiori to Joule Work
items.author: Daniel_Enderli
items.text:
The Evolution of the SAP User Interface: From SAP GUI to Fiori to Joule Work 
 From transactions to intuitive apps to AI-powered collaboration – the SAP user experience is not just changing its appearance. It is changing the way we work. 

 Anyone who has worked with SAP for a long time will remember it: the classic SAP GUI, countless transaction codes, complex screens, and a user interface that was primarily designed to do one thing – provide functionality. 
 But the world has changed. And so have our expectations of enterprise software. 
 Looking back, we can see just how far we have come – and what this evolution means for us as people. 
 1. SAP GUI – The Era of Transactions 
 Throughout the 1990s and well beyond, SAP GUI was the central entry point to business processes in countless companies. 
 The interface was powerful, stable, and designed to support complex business processes. To use SAP efficiently, users had to become familiar with transaction codes, screens, fields, and process logic. 
 People had to learn how SAP worked. 
 Over the years, experienced users developed an enormous amount of knowledge. They knew which transaction to use, which fields mattered, and which steps were required to achieve the desired result. 
 It worked – but shift began in the design of the user experience. 
 Instead of complex transaction screens, the focus moved towards role-based apps, modern design, and more intuitive interaction. The user experience became increasingly aligned with people's tasks and needs. 
 Information was meant to be easier to access. Processes were meant to become more understandable. And SAP was increasingly expected to feel as intuitive as the modern applications we use in everyday life. 
 The key question changed: Not just “How does this transaction work?” but “What task do I want to accomplish?” 
 With Fiori, access to SAP became more modern, flexible, and better suited to different roles and devices. 
 This was more than a new design. It was an important step towards a better user experience and a stronger focus on people. 
 3. Joule Work – From Using Software to AI-Powered Collaboration 
 With generative AI, the next chapter of the SAP user experience is beginning. 
 AI assistants such as Joule make it possible to ask for information in natural language, understand relationships more quickly, and receive intelligent support when completing certain tasks. 
 With Joule Work, SAP is taking this approach further towards an AI-powered work environment. The aim is to bring information and work contexts together more effectively and support tasks across different applications and business processes. 
 Instead of navigating exclusively through menus and applications, users can increasingly describe what they want to achieve. 
 Imagine a typical business scenario: 
 Instead of opening multiple reports and manually compiling data, a user could ask: 
 “Analyze sales performance over the past three months, identify the largest deviations, and summarize the most important areas for action.” 
 The vision is for AI to help users find information, analyze data, and prepare decisions – and, depending on available capabilities and permissions, also assist in executing tasks. 
 People will spend less time searching for information and more time interpreting it and making the right decisions. 
 An important point: Not every task can already be fully automated. The actual benefits depend on the available capabilities, integration with business processes, and the quality of the underlying data. 

 4. The Real Change Is About People 
 The evolution of the SAP user interface is therefore not just a story about technology. 
 It is also a story about how our work is changing. 
 Era What matters most What it means for people 
 SAP GUI Transactions and screens System knowledge and process expertise are essential 
 SAP Fiori Apps and tasks More intuitive interaction and easier access to information 
 Joule Work and AI Intent, context, and assistance Greater focus on analysis, decisions, and collaboration 
 This evolution raises important questions. 
 Which skills will become more important in the future? 
 Knowledge of individual transactions will remain valuable in many areas. At the same time, other skills will become increasingly important: asking the right questions, critically evaluating results, understanding business processes, and using AI effectively. 
 The roles of IT departments, SAP consultants, and process owners are also changing. It is no longer just about configuring systems correctly and training users. Increasingly, it is about designing intelligent workflows, making meaningful use of data, and helping people adapt to a new world of work. 
 And this is where a major challenge lies: New technology alone does not change the way people work. Real value is created only when people understand, trust, and use it effectively. 
 5. What Does This Mean for SAP Transformations? 
 For companies, one important insight emerges: The evolution of the user interface should not be treated as an isolated IT project. 
 Organizations modernizing SAP should also rethink their workflows, employee roles, data quality, and opportunities for automation. 
 Some key questions to consider: 

 Which tasks can be simplified through better user experience and guidance? 

 Where can AI assistants make information available more quickly? 

 Which processes are suitable for further automation? 

 How can we ensure that employees understand and embrace the new possibilities? 

 How do we measure whether productivity, quality, and employee satisfaction are actually improving? 
 Especially in the SAP ecosystem, it will be crucial to develop technology, processes, and people together. 
 Because a modern interface is not an end in itself. It must make work easier, better, and more meaningful. 
 Conclusion: Less Time Operating Systems. More Time Making an Impact. 
 From SAP GUI through SAP Fiori to Joule Work, we are witnessing an evolution that goes far beyond the design of a user interface. 
 We are moving from a world where people had to learn how to operate the system, through a world of intuitive, task-oriented applications, towards a way of working in which AI increasingly understands, assists, and supports tasks. 
 The exciting question is therefore no longer just what the next SAP interface will look like. 
 The real question is: How much more can people achieve when technology takes some of the complexity off their shoulders? 
 The future of SAP will not be measured solely by how intelligent the systems become. It will be measured by how effectively they help people make better decisions, collaborate more efficiently, and focus on what truly matters.

items.title: Already-Posted Off-Cycle Result Re-selected? How Simulation Run Behaves
items.author: Gayathri_V26
items.text:
Introduction 
 Recently, I raised a question in the SAP Community about payroll posting for a terminated employee. I have since found the answer, and I’m sharing it here in case you run into the same behaviour. Original question: Solved: Off-cycle payroll result for terminated employee r... - SAP Community 
 The Scenario 
 We processed an off-cycle payroll run for a terminated employee and posted it to Finance successfully. 
 The FI document was created, and the posting run status showed “ Documents Posted ". 
 Later, we ran the regular monthly payroll posting for all employees in the same payroll area. 
 The terminated employee had no new regular payroll result for the period, which is expected since he was terminated. 
 Even so, the regular posting run selected the same off-cycle result that had already been posted. It looked as if the system was trying to post it again. 
 What We Checked First 
 The employee was not locked at any point. 
 No retroactive calculation was triggered after the off-cycle posting, so no new payroll result was generated. 
 The original off-cycle posting document was not reversed or cancelled. 
 The behavior was reproduced in our test/dev system as well. 
 Nothing in the data pointed to a problem, so I asked whether this was a known issue and whether there was a standard way to resync without reversing the original posting or creating a duplicate. 
 What the Posting Run Showed 
 In the posting item evaluation, the statistics showed: 
 Selected: 3 personnel numbers 
 Evaluated: 2 
 Rejected: 0 
 Skipped: 1 

 The third personnel number, the terminated employee, was flagged with a warning instead of being evaluated like the others. Opening the message gave this: 

 Payroll result has already been evaluated in run 0000023794 
 So the employee was selected for the period, but the system recognized that the result had already been evaluated in the earlier posting run and skipped it. 
 The Solution 
 The behavior was not an error. It comes from how the simulation run works . 
 The simulation run does not primarily validate whether a personnel number has already been posted in a previous posting run. Instead, it simulates the posting of the payroll results selected for the specified payroll period. 
 The simulation option only prevents the creation of a new posting run and FI document. It does not act as a filter to exclude employees whose payroll results have already been posted. 
 So when the terminated employee appeared in the selection, that didn’t mean the system would post him a second time. The selection showed everything that fell within the period, including a result that had already been posted. 
 What Happened in the Live Run 
 When we executed the live posting run , the system posted only the correct amount. There was no duplicate posting and no need to reverse the original document or resync anything. 
 Key Takeaways 
 Being selected is not the same as being posted. An employee can appear in the selection and still be skipped. 
 Don’t use the simulation output as a duplicate check. 
 Simulation only suppresses the new posting run and FI document. It does not exclude results that were already posted. 
 Read the message on the skipped employee. “Payroll result has already been evaluated in run …” tells you which earlier run holds the result. 
 The live run determines what is actually posted. In our case, only the correct amount was posted. 
 Verify after the live run. Confirm the new posting run and its FI documents, and check that the earlier off-cycle FI document is unchanged. 
 Conclusion 
 If an already-posted off-cycle result for a terminated employee shows up again in a later posting run, don’t assume a duplicate will be created, and don’t reverse the original posting because of what the selection shows. Check the message on the skipped employee, run the live posting, and verify the resulting documents. 
 I hope this saves you some troubleshooting time. If you have seen similar behavior or know more about the selection logic behind it, please share it in the comments.
