items.title: From blind spot to threat signal: feed SAP Application Vulnerability Report into Microsoft Sentinel
items.author: Fabian_Richter
items.text:
co-authored by Martin Pankraz 
 Dear community, 
 Since April 2026, your custom BAIP apps have officially graduated: they are now first-class targets for the hacker community in software supply chain attacks. The customers who ran vulnerability scanning at the time spotted the exposure fastest and rolled out SAP's fixes within hours. Everyone else found out the hard way. According to Microsoft’s latest digital defense report 2026: “Open-source supply chain compromise” is the number one emerging threat for the next year (see page 36, threat landscape). 
 Knowing which CVE sits in your custom app on BAIP is only half the job. You also need to know whether someone is actively exploiting it right now - and that signal lives in your SOC, not in a scan report. 
 A mental model to dissect this space 
 Shift Left - secure code before it ships (static analysis, dependency scanning in your pipeline). 
 Shield Right - protect and monitor the running app at runtime. 
 The missing link - take the application vulnerability report's runtime findings and correlate them everything else happening across your estate using your SIEM application. 
 This article is about that third piece. The application vulnerability report tells you a known CVE is live in a BAIP custom app. Microsoft Sentinel for SAP tells you the same tenant just saw a suspicious Entra ID sign-in, lateral movement, and sensitive SAP data download. Alone, each is noise. Together, they are an incident! See below incident graph and timeline informed by Microsoft Sentinel for SAP on the Microsoft Defender portal from an SAP attack replay. 

 What the application vulnerability report gives you 
 SAP's first-party application vulnerability report continuously identifies known CVEs in the custom applications you run on BAIP - no agent to deploy, no separate scanner to license. It is the authoritative, SAP-sourced view of what is vulnerable in your code. If you are new to the Application Vulnerability Report, this is the fastest way to see your BAIP custom-code exposure. 
 Bringing it into Microsoft Sentinel for SAP BAIP 
 With the integration of the application vulnerability report into the Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP BAIP, your existing BAIP telemetry is enriched with these CVE findings. See below Screenshot from the Microsoft Sentinel Incident overview on the correlation of the SAP BAIP audit log and the Application Vulnerability Report findings. 
 It features the vulnerable CAP app which was used during the red team event at DSAG TechXChange 2026 showing AI prompt injection attacks. 

 The vulnerability signal can now be correlated with the rest of your security data. 
 Beyond the automatic correlation , you get out-of-the-box visualizations for querying and continuous monitoring, built for the people who own BAIP security day to day. If you already run the application vulnerability report but have never pushed its findings into a SIEM , this is the step that turns a periodic report into a live detection surface. See below visuals produced from the API output of the new vulnerability report service. 

 A mesh of screenshots from the updated workbook on Microsoft Sentinel for SAP 
 Comparing with shift-left approaches 
 GitHub Advanced Security is one sample of tackling vulnerabilities with the shift-left approach during design time till your DevOps pipelines and before code is put into production. It is excellent at what it does: finding vulnerabilities in source code before it ever ships. It scans your repositories, flags vulnerable dependencies, and catches secrets in commits. 
 The a pplication vulnerability report answers a different question . It does not look at your repository; it looks at what is running on BTP and tells you which known CVEs are live in production right now. 
 GitHub Advanced Security secures the code on its way in. The application vulnerability report, correlated in Sentinel, tells you whether a live vulnerability is being exploited . They are complementary: one hardens the pipeline, the other watches the runtime. 
 What's next? 
 We are expanding the correlation content : more out-of-the-box detection rules mapping application vulnerability report findings to active-exploitation signals, and richer workbooks for BAIP security personas. Expect tighter mapping between specific CVE classes and attacker behaviors that typically follow them. 
 In addition to that we would like to hear from you what you need most from the BAIP vulnerability space. 
 Get started today 
 Enable the application vulnerability report for your BAIP custom apps. 
 Deploy the latest Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP BAIP v 3.2.1. 
 Turn on the application vulnerability report connector (preview*) using the service key , so CVE findings flow into Sentinel for SAP BTP. 
 Deploy the workbook “ BAIP Activity ” and analytic rules shipped with the Sentinel solution for SAP BAIP 
 Discover your current vulnerable apps from the workbook, and watch for correlated incidents, where a known vulnerability meets suspicious runtime activity. 
 Shift Left secures the code. Shield Right protects the runtime. Correlating the application vulnerability report in your SIEM closes the loop between the two. 
 * the connector remains in preview while the Application Vulnerability Report service is in Beta . 
 Closing the loop 
 Custom applications on SAP BAIP need continuous vulnerability visibility - but isolated findings are only the beginning. By bringing SAP application vulnerability report findings into Microsoft Sentinel, your SOC can connect known CVEs in production with suspicious activity across the broader environment and investigate incidents with the context they need. 
 Shift Left and Shield Right serve different, complementary purposes: solutions such as GitHub Advanced Security help secure code throughout development and delivery, while the SAP application vulnerability report identifies known vulnerabilities in applications already running on BAIP. Correlating those runtime findings in Sentinel closes the gap between vulnerable code and active threats. 
 Through close collaboration between SAP and Microsoft engineering, Microsoft Sentinel for SAP BAIP now delivers a broader, more actionable view of application risk. 
 Now we want to hear from you : which detections, analytics rules, or workbook insights would make the biggest difference for your SAP BAIP security operations? Share your priorities in the comments or reach out to us directly. 
 Cheers 
 Fabian and Martin

items.title: Your AI agents are only as good as the knowledge behind them
items.author: Jelisaveta_Nikolic
items.text:
Enterprises are deploying AI agents faster than they can teach them how the business actually works. 
 An agent assigned to approve a purchase order, screen a customer, or close the books doesn't fail because the model isn't capable. It fails because it doesn't know your rules: the approval threshold for EMEA orders above €100k, the exception that requires board sign-off, the compliance step that is never optional. That knowledge rarely lives anywhere an agent can reach it. It is scattered across 500-page policy documents, SharePoint sites, Confluence pages, email threads, and the heads of the three people who have been there long enough to remember why the rule exists. 
 So teams do the only thing they can: they hand-curate a bundle of documents and paste it into each agent's prompt. It works for a demo. Then a rule changes, the bundle goes stale, two departments encode the same policy differently, and nobody discovers the drift until an audit does. Every new agent starts the same context-gathering from scratch. The promise of the agentic enterprise stalls, not on the agents, but on the fractured, static knowledge underneath them. 
 This is the gap SAP Company Memory preview is built to close. 
 A governed knowledge layer, not another document store 
 SAP Company Memory is a governed knowledge layer that delivers an organization's business rules, policies, and institutional knowledge to AI agents and to people at the moment of decision. 
 The difference from a wiki or knowledge base is structural. Instead of storing documents and hoping consumers can find the right passage, SAP Company Memory turns scattered rules into atoms: small, consistent, retrievable units. Each atom carries three things: 
 Purpose: why the rule exists 
 Scope: when it applies (region, role, process, system) 
 Rule: the exact governing statement 
 Every atom keeps a citation back to its source document and page, so any answer can be traced to its origin. Atoms carry hierarchy too. A global sanctions rule, a company-wide policy, a regional exception, a customer-specific term can all coexist, and the right one surfaces for the right context, the way a well-briefed employee would apply it. 
 Because the knowledge is structured once and governed centrally, it can be consumed many ways: 
 Agents connect at runtime over MCP and retrieve exactly the rules relevant to the decision in front of them, with no manual SOP-to-prompt translation and no vendor lock-in. 
 Developers query and export structured rule sets through a CLI at build time. 
 People ask questions in plain language and get a specific, cited answer back. 
 And when rules collide, for example "orders below €20 need approval" in one document and "orders below €20 don't" in another, SAP Company Memory scans the whole corpus, surfaces the conflict, and walks an owner through resolving it before any agent ever consumes a contradiction. 
 The same layer that governs agents answers your people's questions too 
 Here is the part that surprises teams: the knowledge you structure to make agents reliable turns out to be exactly what your people have been missing. 
 The rules buried in that 500-page document weren't only invisible to agents. They were invisible to the new hire on day three, to the process owner trying to work out what breaks if a policy changes, to the employee who asks a colleague and still gets it wrong. Make the knowledge explicit, governed, and queryable, and the human side lights up: 
 Instant, cited answers to policy questions. "What's our approval threshold for EMEA orders above €100k?" returns a specific atom with its source, not a link to a PDF to go read. 
 Onboarding in days, not months. New hires query SAP Company Memory instead of shadowing colleagues to absorb tribal knowledge. 
 Impact analysis before a change. "What breaks if we change this rule?" is answered in seconds, not weeks of manual cross-referencing. 
 Authoring by the people who own the rules. Business owners write and maintain rules in natural language, rather than filing a ticket with a technical team. 
 Knowledge that survives people leaving. Institutional memory becomes explicit and retrievable instead of walking out the door. 
 The two audiences reinforce each other. Humans author and validate the rules; agents consume them at runtime; what we learn from execution feeds back to the people maintaining them. The knowledge layer gets more valuable the more it is used. 
 The foundation is already in place 
 A business-rules layer for agents is only as good as the rules that feed it. The hard part is not building the retrieval layer; it is cold-starting a corpus of real, validated enterprise rules that agents can actually rely on. 
 SAP enters this with a foundation already assembled: 
 Process models that specify how a business should run, built from two decades of enterprise process design in SAP Signavio. 
 Execution data from business process intelligence and S/4HANA that shows how it actually runs, so rules can be grounded in reality, not just asserted. 
 Domain expertise packaged across thousands of SAP reference models and content packages. 
 The business owners themselves, already working inside the tools where this knowledge lives. 
 Where we are, and where we're headed 
 SAP Company Memory is in the hands of selected design partners today, through an early-access program running on SAP Signavio infrastructure. We are deliberately building this with customers rather than announcing it finished; the beta partners are shaping ingestion, governance, and the human query experience as we go. 
 Broader availability follows as that validation matures. We will share specifics on timing as we get closer; for now, the direction is clear and the foundation is in customers' hands. 
 What we are building toward is a self-enriching organizational memory: a knowledge layer that humans trust for answers, agents rely on to execute correctly, and systems draw on for consistency, one that gets sharper every time it is used. 
 Want to follow along, or get involved? 
 If your organization is deploying AI agents into business processes and running into the knowledge gap described here, we'd like to talk. We're expanding the design-partner program and are especially interested in teams working through agent governance, onboarding, and compliance. 
 Want to know more? Feel free to reach out!

items.title: SAP PLMSI & Clean Core
items.author: Stella_Neser
items.text:
– Positioning PLM System Integration within the Clean Core Extensibility Model 
 Clean Core is a central architectural principle of SAP that aims to keep the SAP core as close to the standard as possible. Extensions should be implemented exclusively through released, upgrade-stable interfaces and extension points. This ensures that system upgrades can be carried out smoothly and that customer-specific adaptations remain maintainable and future-proof in the long term. 
 In the context of SAP PLM System Integration (PLMSI), the standardized integration component for bidirectional data transfer between SAP S/4HANA and an external PLM system (e.g. Siemens Teamcenter), the question arises as to how customer-specific extensions can be implemented in a clean-core-compliant manner. 
 This Block-Post explains the clean core extensibility levels, positions the PLMSI extension mechanisms within this framework, and provides clear guidance for implementation practice. 
 Contents 
 The SAP Clean Core Extensibility Model 
 Extension Patterns: On-Stack and Side-by-Side 
 SAP PLMSI in the Context Clean Core 
 3.1 BAdIs as Released Extension Points 
 3.2 Categories of PLMSI BAdIs 
 3.3 Configuration vs. Implementation 
 Positioning PLMSI Extensions with Clean Core Levels 
 Future-Proofing and Evolution 
 Conclusion 

 1. The SAP Clean Core Extensibility Model 
 SAP defines four extensibility levels (A through D) that describe the degree of clean core compliance of an extension. The higher the level, the more upgrade-stable and future-proof the implementation. 

 Level 
 Description 
 Clean Core? 

 Level A 
 Extensions based on released APIs and extension points. Development with ABAP Cloud (SAP Build) or side-by-side on SAP BTP. Highest upgrade stability. 
 ✅ Yes – Target state 

 Level B 
 Extensions using classic APIs and frameworks (e.g. BAPIs, classic BAdIs) that are not formally tagged as "released" but are recognized as upgrade-stable. 
 ✅ Yes 

 Level C 
 Use of internal SAP objects that are not officially released. Conditionally clean, provided that change-log monitoring is set up. 
 ⚠️ Conditional 

 Level D 
 Modifications, implicit enhancements, direct table writes, or non-recommended extension technologies. Not upgrade-stable. 
 ❌ No 
 The following diagram shows how clean core levels map to SAP standard objects: 

 Figure 1: Clean core levels mapped to SAP standard objects 
 Source: SAP – Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud (2024) 
 2. Extension Patterns: On-Stack and Side-by-Side 
 SAP distinguishes two fundamental extension patterns for SAP Cloud ERP Private: 
 A) On-Stack Extensibility (directly on SAP S/4HANA): 
 Adapting and extending standard applications (e.g. custom fields, data model extensions) 
 Creating custom full-stack applications with custom UI, application logic, and persistence 
 Creating and consuming APIs and events for integration connectivity 
 B) Side-by-Side Extensibility (on SAP Business Technology Platform): 
 Developing custom full-stack or mobile applications 
 Automating tasks and processes across system boundaries 
 Using workflows, rules, and central entry points 
 The following diagram provides an overview of the extension patterns: 

 Figure 2: Extension use case patterns for SAP Cloud ERP Private 
 Source: SAP – Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud (2024) 

 3. SAP PLMSI in the Context of Clean Core 
 3.1 BAdIs as Released Extension Points 
 SAP PLM System Integration (PLMSI) provides a wide range of documented BAdIs (Business Add-Ins) that are designated as official extension points for customer-specific adaptations. These BAdIs are documented in the SAP Configuration Guide for PLMSI and therefore belong to the released extension points of the SAP standard. 
 The use of these BAdIs is clean-core-compliant and corresponds to Level A or Level B of the SAP extensibility model, provided that only released or classic APIs and objects are used within the BAdI implementation. 
 3.2 Categories of PLMSI BAdIs 
 The PLMSI BAdIs can be categorized as follows: 
 Post-Processing BAdIs: Customer-specific post-processing steps after successful standard processing of inbound messages (e.g. for material master, document master, change objects, bills of material). 
 Read Extension Fields BAdIs: Enrichment of outbound data with additional customer-specific fields during read access (e.g. BAdI /PLMF/BD_PV_READ_EXTN_FLD for material master data). 
 Custom Conversion BAdIs: Definition of custom conversion logic for data formats (e.g. date formats, units of measure). 
 Custom Logic BAdIs: Complete implementation of custom processing logic as a replacement for the standard integration. These BAdIs offer methods for Maintain (write) and Read (read) and allow the creation of entirely custom SAP objects or the implementation of deviating business logic. 
 Selection Condition BAdIs: Adaptation of selection conditions for specific object types (e.g. routings). 
 Inbound Request BAdIs: Adjustment of data in inbound maintain requests before standard processing, as well as modification of the response before it is returned to the external system. 

 Note: The number of avialabe BAdI extention points varies depending on the PLMSI version and feature pack. 
 3.3 Configuration vs. Implementation 
 A significant portion of PLMSI functionality can be covered purely through configuration – without any code development. This includes, among other things, scenario definitions, attribute mappings, conversion rules, and the assignment of processing pipelines. 
 For requirements beyond this – such as complex business logic, customer-specific validations, or the integration of additional SAP objects – the BAdIs described above are available. This combination of configuration and BAdI-based extension is architecturally intentional and fully clean-core-compliant. 
 4. Positioning PLMSI Extensions within Clean Core Levels 

 Extension Type 
 Clean Core Level 
 Assessment 

 PLMSI configuration (scenario setup, attribute mappings, conversion rules) 
 Level A 
 ✅ Fully compliant 

 BAdI implementation using released/classic APIs and objects 
 Level A / B 
 ✅ Compliant 

 BAdI implementation using internal SAP objects 
 Level C 
 ⚠️ Conditionally compliant – change-log monitoring recommended 

 Direct modification of SAP standard (not recommended) 
 Level D 
 ❌ Not compliant 
 5. Future-Proofing and Evolution 
 Since the PLMSI BAdIs are provided as released extension points, upgrade safety is should be ensured. SAP updates typically do not affect BAdI implementations, as the BAdI framework ensures a clean separation between standard code and customer extensions. 
 Furthermore, it is possible that future PLMSI versions may incorporate into the standard some extensions that are currently realized through BAdIs. This would prospectively reduce customer-specific implementation effort and further increase the degree of standardization. 
 SAP regularly releases new released APIs and BAdIs. For a current overview, the following resources are recommended: 
 SAP Road Map Explorer for PLM System Integration 
 SAP Business Accelerator Hub (for released APIs) 
 Cloudification Repository Viewer (for classic APIs) 
 SAP Help Portal – PLMSI Configuration Guide 
 6. Conclusion 
 The use of SAP PLMSI BAdIs is clean-core-compliant. SAP has intentionally provided these extension points to enable customer-specific integration requirements within a future-proof, upgrade-stable architectural framework. 
 For implementation, the following clear recommendations apply: 
 Prioritize configuration – wherever possible, address requirements through PLMSI configuration. 
 Use BAdIs with released objects – this corresponds to Level A/B and is unconditionally clean-core-compliant. 
 Use internal objects only when necessary – and set up change-log monitoring in that case (Level C). 
 Avoid modifications – direct interventions in the SAP standard are not clean-core-compliant and jeopardize upgrade capability (Level D). 
 Sources

 https://www.sap.com/documents/2024/09/20aece06-d87e-0010-bca6-c68f7e60039b.html

 [4] SAP Learning – Exploring How to Make Extensions Clean Core Compliant

items.title: Bringing SAP BAIP, Kyma Runtime to China: Expanding Cloud-Native Development Capabilities
items.author: TiaXu
items.text:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is now available in China, extending the local SAP BAIP portfolio with a managed Kubernetes-based runtime for cloud-native applications, microservices, and SAP extensions. 
 Bringing Cloud-Native Innovation Closer to Chinese Customers 
 Modern enterprises increasingly need to extend business applications, connect systems, and deliver new digital capabilities without introducing unnecessary complexity into their core landscapes. 
 SAP BAIP in China already offers Cloud Foundry runtime as a mature PaaS option for deploying applications using buildpack-based workflows. Kyma runtime addresses a different set of needs. Built on the open-source Kyma project and Kubernetes, it gives development teams direct access to container-based workloads, serverless functions, and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem—without restriction on programming language or framework. Any workload that can be containerized can run on Kyma runtime. 
 On June 2, 2026, SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime became available in China (North 3), followed by China (Shanghai) on July 10, 2026—making this managed cloud-native application runtime available through the local BTPEA commercial offering across both regions. 
 What Is Now Available? 
 SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is offered under the BTPEA commercial model , under SKU 8016044 (the customer-facing BTPEA SKU), with the following service plans: 

 Service: Display Name Service Plan: Display Name Available Data Center 
 Kyma Runtime Kyma Runtime Alibaba Cloud China (Shanghai) — cn40 
 Kyma Runtime Kyma Runtime Azure China (North 3) — cn20 
 Customers and partners can explore the service and its regional availability through SAP Discovery Center: 
 China (North 3) — Kyma Runtime 
 China (Shanghai) — Kyma Runtime 

 The China BTPEA price list lists the Standard plan as a billable plan for SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime. 
 Why This Matters 
 A Managed, Flexible Foundation for Cloud-Native Applications 
 Running Kubernetes in-house requires ongoing investment in cluster management, upgrades, security patching, and infrastructure operations. SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime removes that burden: SAP manages the underlying platform, while customers retain full control over their applications and workloads. Development teams can focus on building business capabilities instead of maintaining infrastructure. 
 Compared to Cloud Foundry runtime, Kyma offers a meaningfully different development model. Cloud Foundry abstracts the runtime through buildpacks, which works well for deploying Java or Node.js applications quickly but limits what you can run and how. Kyma places no such constraints: any containerized workload runs on Kyma regardless of language or framework, and teams have direct access to Kubernetes-native tooling—Helm for packaging, custom resource definitions, fine-grained resource configuration, and the broader CNCF ecosystem. For teams building modern cloud-native applications or needing precise control over their workloads, this flexibility is a significant advantage. 
 The two runtimes are complementary. Cloud Foundry remains a solid choice for buildpack-based application deployment; Kyma is the better fit when container-native flexibility, polyglot development, or Kubernetes ecosystem tooling is a requirement. 
 Extending SAP Applications with Event-Driven Integration 
 Kyma runtime includes a built-in Eventing component that allows applications to subscribe directly to business events from SAP S/4HANA and other SAP systems—so an extension can react to a sales order creation, a goods movement, or a master data change in real time, without polling or point-to-point connections. Having this capability integrated into the runtime means teams can start building event-driven extensions without separately provisioning and configuring a messaging service. 
 Combined with serverless functions and a built-in API Gateway, this makes it practical to build lightweight, loosely coupled extensions that sit alongside the SAP core rather than inside it. Custom logic evolves independently, upgrade cycles are decoupled, and the core system remains stable. 
 For scenarios that go beyond SAP-to-SAP integration—connecting third-party systems, orchestrating multi-step workflows, or building net-new business applications—Kyma provides the same Kubernetes-based foundation with the flexibility to incorporate any service or technology the use case requires. 
 Expanding the Local SAP BAIP Development Portfolio 
 With Kyma runtime available in China (North 3) and China (Shanghai), customers gain an additional runtime option within the local SAP BAIP portfolio. 
 This is particularly relevant for teams building containerized applications, API-based integrations, event-driven extensions, and microservices that complement SAP business solutions. 
 The availability of Kyma runtime broadens the technology choices available to the China ecosystem and provides another foundation for cloud-native application development.

items.author: TiaXu
items.text:
SAP BAIP, ABAP Environment is now available in China, giving customers and partners a new way to build cloud-ready ABAP applications and extensions on SAP Business AI Platform. 
 A New Milestone for ABAP Development in China 
 On October 15, 2026, SAP BAIP, ABAP environment was released in China, marking an important milestone in expanding SAP's cloud development capabilities for the local market. 
 ABAP has long been central to the development and extension of SAP business applications. As enterprises modernize their SAP landscapes, they need ways to preserve their ABAP expertise and existing investments while adopting cloud-ready development practices. 
 SAP BAIP, ABAP environment addresses this need by providing a cloud-optimized ABAP platform for developing and running applications and extensions. It enables customers to reuse ABAP skills and assets, build side-by-side extensions, and decouple custom code from the digital core—supporting a Clean Core approach and more flexible innovation cycles. 
 With its availability in China, these capabilities can now be accessed through the local SAP BAIP commercial offering.

This new offering complements the existing regions on SAP Cloud Infrastructure, AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. 
 Why This Matters 
 Supporting Clean Core and Cloud Transformation 
 A key benefit of SAP BAIP, ABAP environment is its support for side-by-side extensibility. Customers can build custom applications and extensions separately from their SAP S/4HANA core, helping reduce coupling between custom code and core business processes. 
 This approach supports a more upgrade-stable architecture and gives organizations greater flexibility to evolve their extensions independently. It is particularly relevant for enterprises pursuing SAP S/4HANA modernization and Clean Core initiatives. 
 Building on Existing ABAP Expertise 
 Cloud transformation does not mean leaving existing development expertise behind. By providing a cloud-based ABAP development and runtime environment, SAP helps customers and partners continue to leverage their ABAP knowledge while adopting the ABAP Cloud development model. 
 This creates opportunities to modernize custom applications, develop new business capabilities, and extend SAP solutions using familiar skills and a cloud-ready foundation. 
 Expanding Local Access to SAP BAIP Innovation 
 Making the service available in both China (North 3) and China (Shanghai) expands the options available to customers and partners building on SAP BAIP in China. 
 It also strengthens the local portfolio of development capabilities that support enterprise application modernization, partner innovation, and the evolution of SAP-centric business solutions. 
 A new chapter for cloud-ready ABAP development in China has begun.

items.author: TiaXu
items.text:
SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 现已在中国正式上线，为客户和合作伙伴在 SAP Business AI Platform (SAP BAIP) 上构建面向云端的 ABAP 应用与扩展提供了新的途径。 
 ABAP 开发在中国迎来新里程碑 
 2026 年 10 月 15 日，SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 在中国正式发布，标志着 SAP 在本地市场扩展云端开发能力的重要里程碑。 
 ABAP 长期以来是 SAP 业务应用开发与扩展的核心。随着企业推进 SAP 系统的现代化改造，他们需要在采用云端开发实践的同时，保留现有的 ABAP 专业积累与既有投资。 
 SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 通过提供云优化的 ABAP 平台来满足这一需求，支持应用与扩展程序的开发和运行。它使客户能够复用 ABAP 技能与资产、构建 side-by-side 扩展，并将自定义代码与数字核心解耦——助力 Clean Core 方法落地，加快创新迭代节奏。 
 随着该服务在中国上线，上述能力现已通过本地 SAP BAIP 正式对外提供。 
 现已提供哪些内容？ 
 该服务基于 BTPEA 商业模式 提供，SKU 为 8016044 （面向客户的 BTPEA SKU），包含以下服务计划：

 为何重要 
 支持 Clean Core 与云端转型 
 SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 的一大核心优势在于支持 side-by-side 扩展。客户可以在独立于 SAP S/4HANA 核心的环境中构建自定义应用与扩展，有效降低自定义代码与核心业务流程之间的耦合度。 
 这种方式有助于构建更具升级稳定性的架构，使组织能够更灵活地独立演进其扩展程序，尤其适合正在推进 SAP S/4HANA 现代化与 Clean Core 战略的企业。 
 延续现有 ABAP 专业积累

 这为延伸现有能力、开发新业务功能、以及基于云端基础扩展 SAP 解决方案打开了新的空间。 
 扩展本地 SAP BAIP 创新渠道 
 在中国（华北3）和中国（上海）同步上线，进一步扩展了中国客户和合作伙伴在 SAP BAIP 上的选择空间。 
 这也强化了支持企业应用现代化、合作伙伴创新以及 SAP 核心业务解决方案演进的本地开发能力组合。

items.title: SAP BAIP Kyma runtime 正式落地中国：扩展云原生开发能力
items.author: TiaXu
items.text:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 现已在中国正式上线，在本地 SAP BAIP 上提供了一个托管 Kubernetes 运行时，支持云原生应用、微服务及 SAP 扩展开发。 
 云原生创新能力走近中国客户 
 现代企业越来越需要在不增加核心系统复杂度的前提下，扩展业务应用、连接各类系统、并持续交付新的数字化能力。 
 SAP BAIP 在中国已提供 Cloud Foundry runtime 作为成熟的 PaaS 选项，适用于基于 buildpack 工作流的应用部署。Kyma runtime 则面向不同的需求场景。它基于开源 Kyma 项目和 Kubernetes 构建，让开发团队可以直接使用容器化工作负载、Serverless Functions 以及更广泛的 Kubernetes 生态系统——不限编程语言和框架。任何可容器化的工作负载均可在 Kyma runtime 上运行。 
 2026 年 6 月 2 日，SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）率先上线，随后于 2026 年 7 月 10 日扩展至中国（上海）——通过本地 BTPEA 商业模式，在两个区域全面开放。 
 现已提供哪些内容？ 
 该服务基于 BTPEA 商业模式 提供，SKU 为 8016044 （面向客户的 BTPEA SKU），包含以下服务计划： 
 服务名称 服务计划名称 可用数据中心 
 Kyma Runtime Kyma Runtime Alibaba Cloud 中国（上海）— cn40 
 Kyma Runtime Kyma Runtime Azure 中国（华北3）— cn20 
 客户和合作伙伴可通过 SAP Discovery Center 查看服务及其可用地区： 
 中国（华北3）— Kyma runtime 
 中国（上海）— Kyma runtime 

 中国 BTPEA 价格表 中列出了 SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 的 Standard 计费计划。 
 为何重要 
 托管、灵活的云原生应用基础平台 
 自建 Kubernetes 需要持续投入集群管理、版本升级、安全补丁和基础设施运维。SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 消除了这一负担：SAP 负责底层平台的管理，客户则完全掌控自己的应用和工作负载。开发团队可以专注于构建业务能力，而不是维护基础设施。 
 与 Cloud Foundry runtime 相比，Kyma 提供了一种截然不同的开发模式。Cloud Foundry 通过 buildpack 对运行时进行抽象，这种方式非常适合快速部署 Java 或 Node.js 应用，但对能运行什么、如何运行有一定限制。Kyma 没有这类约束：无论使用何种语言或框架，任何容器化工作负载都可以在 Kyma 上运行，团队还可以直接使用 Kubernetes 原生工具链——包括用于打包的 Helm、自定义资源定义、精细化资源配置，以及更广泛的 CNCF 生态系统。对于构建现代云原生应用或需要精确控制工作负载的团队而言，这种灵活性是显著的优势。 
 两种运行时相辅相成。Cloud Foundry 仍然是 buildpack 应用部署的可靠选择；当团队需要容器原生的灵活性、多语言支持或 Kubernetes 生态工具时，Kyma 则更为适合。 
 通过事件驱动集成扩展 SAP 应用 
 Kyma runtime 内置了 Eventing 组件，允许应用直接订阅来自 SAP S/4HANA 及其他 SAP 系统的业务事件——扩展程序可以实时响应销售订单创建、货物移动或主数据变更等事件，无需轮询或点对点连接。由于该能力已集成在运行时中，团队无需单独配置消息服务即可开始构建事件驱动扩展。 
 结合 Serverless Functions 和内置 API Gateway，这使得构建轻量、松耦合的扩展程序变得切实可行——这些扩展与 SAP 核心系统并行运行，而非嵌入其中。自定义逻辑独立演进，升级周期解耦，核心系统保持稳定。 
 对于超出 SAP 间集成范畴的场景——连接第三方系统、编排多步骤工作流或构建全新业务应用——Kyma 提供了同样的 Kubernetes 基础平台，并具备灵活引入任何所需服务或技术的能力。 
 扩展本地 SAP BAIP 开发组合 
 随着 Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）和中国（上海）相继上线，中国客户在 SAP BAIP 上多了一个可用的运行时选择。

items.title: Using AI to Audit SAP Master Data Before It Becomes a Project Risk
items.author: Eniehues
items.text:
Hi everyone, 
 In several SAP projects I’ve managed (ECC to S/4HANA migrations and AMS operations), master data quality issues tend to appear late, usually during testing, cutover, or right after go-live, when they’re the most expensive to fix. 
 I’m exploring an approach that combines standard SAP tables with an AI agent to run a master data health check earlier in the project, and I’d like to hear how others are handling this. 
 The idea in short: 
 Extract key tables using read-only access (e.g., SE16N), such as MARA, MARC, MEAN, BUT000, LFA1, LFB1, LFM1, KNA1, ADRC, ADR6, MAST, PLKO, and MKAL. 
 Run automated checks, for example: 
 Duplicates: vendors, customers, or business partners with the same name, address, phone, or email; materials with the same GTIN/EAN 
 Missing master data: in-house produced materials without a BOM, routing, or production version 
 Best-practice violations: vendors without the duplicate invoice check flag (LFB1-REPRF), or payment terms that differ between company code (LFB1-ZTERM) and purchasing organization (LFM1-ZTERM) 
 Use AI for fuzzy matching (e.g., “ACME Corp.” vs. “Acme Corporation”), prioritizing findings by business impact, and explaining them in plain language. 
 My questions to the community: 
 Are you already using AI or machine learning for master data quality checks in SAP? If so, which tools or approaches have worked best? 
 Are there other high-value checks you would add to this list? 
 How do you handle data privacy when extracting master data (addresses, emails, bank details) for analysis outside SAP? 
 Have you seen SAP MDG or SAP Business AI features covering these scenarios natively? 
 Any experiences or recommendations would be greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance!

items.title: IM52 error "Annual budget less than distributed budget" - fix with IMCAOV?
items.author: DW2023
items.text:
Hi experts, 
 We need advice on an Investment Management budget issue. 
 We created a new AFE (WBS element) and transferred part of the budget from an existing AFE to it. We now need to reduce the overall budget of the original AFE by about 250,000 (from 6,000,000 to 5,750,000) in IM52, but the save is blocked. 
 The AFE is assigned to program position PROG1 (several other WBS elements are also assigned to it) in investment program CAPEX, approval year 2025. The AFE's annual budgets are FY2025 250,000 and FY2026 5,750,000. The FY2026 amount came from the budget carryforward at WBS level (CJCO). 
 Reducing the overall budget first gave BQ154/BQ155 because the annual budgets still totaled 6,000,000. We activated annual budgeting in the budget profiles, but reducing the FY2025 annual budget now fails with: 
 "Annual budget 2026 less than distributed budget, PROG1: 0.00 < 26,000,000.00" 
 In IM53 (CAPEX/2025), position PROG1 shows: Period Current budget Distributed Distributable 
 FY2025 88,000,000 26,500,000 61,500,000 
 FY2026 0 26,000,000 -26,000,000 
 SAP Support confirmed that budget was carried forward at WBS level (CJCO) but not at program level and suggested running IMCAOV or maintaining FY2026 budget manually in IM32. 
 We plan to run IMCAOV for investment program CAPEX and position PROG1. 
 Our questions: 
 Which approval year and sender fiscal year should we enter: approval year 2025 with sender fiscal year 2025? Should the "budget as supplement/return" option be selected, and what difference does it make? 
 What does IMCAOV change, and where should we check the result after the run (for example IM53 period 2026, IM33, or a report)? How can we confirm the inconsistency is fully fixed? 
 After IMCAOV, what are the steps to complete the AFE reduction without getting BQ154/BQ155 again? Is this the right order: reduce the AFE's annual budget in IM52 (2025 and 2026), then reduce its overall budget? 
 Should the budget profiles be switched back to overall-only afterward, and would that cause BQ154/BQ155 for future reductions? 
 If we enter only position PROG1, will IMCAOV also process all program positions below it? Since other positions have the same issue, should we run it for the whole program instead? 
 Is there any risk in running IMCAOV now, months after the fiscal year change, when FY2026 budgets have already been distributed and used? What should we check before the live run, and what should we look for in the test run output? 
 Any guidance would be much appreciated. Thank you!

items.title: BTP Cockpit dashboard improvements, plus MCP-based code review in BAS and user maintenance
items.author: wjamili
items.text:
We run several subaccounts on SAP BTP across dev, test, and prod, and I’d like input on three topics. 
 1. BTP Cockpit dashboard improvements 
 The current cockpit overview works for single subaccounts, but for day-to-day administration we’re missing a few things. I’d like to know whether these exist (or are on the roadmap) and what workarounds people use: 
 A cross-subaccount overview of entitlements and quota consumption, with threshold alerts 
 A health view of service instances and bindings (failed, outdated, or orphaned) 
 An expiry view for service keys, certificates, and destination credentials 
 Role collection and user assignment overview, with a filter for inactive users 
 Cost and consumption trends per subaccount or directory 
 Customizable tiles or saved views per admin role 
 Audit log highlights on the landing page (recent role changes, new service bindings) 
 Are others using the Cloud Management Service, the Usage Data Management service, or custom dashboards built on the BTP CLI and APIs? Which gaps did you fill that way? 
 2. MCP server for code review in SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) 
 I’m exploring Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to support code review directly in BAS, for CAP (Node.js/Java), UI5/Fiori, and MTA projects. Specifically: 
 Which MCP servers or packages are you using or recommending for SAP development (for example, CAP, UI5, or Fiori tooling)? 
 Can a general code-review or linting MCP server be combined with them in BAS dev spaces, and are there restrictions on installing or running them there? 
 How do you handle security and governance (allowed MCP servers, secrets, data leaving the dev space)? 
 Do you have a review checklist or prompt setup for CAP models, service handlers, mta.yaml , xs-security.json , and UI5 manifests? 
 Security review 
 Can an MCP server (or a combination of one with tools like Semgrep, ESLint security plugins, or npm audit ) check for common issues in BAS, such as injection in custom handlers, hardcoded secrets, and insecure dependencies? 
 How do you review CAP-specific security: missing or too-broad @requires and @restrict annotations, unprotected services or actions, and unintended @CDS .query.limit or exposure of sensitive fields? 
 How do you validate xs-security.json (scopes, role templates, over-privileged roles), approuter and CORS settings, and destination or credential handling in mta.yaml ? 
 Is there a way to check UI5/Fiori apps for XSS risks, unsafe eval or inline scripts, and CSP issues? 
 How do you scan for vulnerable or outdated npm and Maven dependencies, and for secrets in default-env.json , .env , or .cdsrc files before commit? 
 Can these checks run in the dev space and also in the CI/CD pipeline (for example with SAP Continuous Integration and Delivery), so findings are consistent across both? 
 3. MCP or automation for user maintenance 
 For user and authorization maintenance (SAP Cloud Identity Services / IAS, XSUAA role collections, subaccount members), I’d like to know: 
 Is there an MCP server or package that wraps the BTP CLI, the Authorization & Trust Management APIs, or SCIM for read and write operations? 
 How do you keep AI-assisted user maintenance safe: read-only by default, approval steps, audit trail? 
 Any experience automating recurring tasks like onboarding or offboarding, role collection assignment, or removing inactive users? 
 Any pointers, blog posts, GitHub repos, or lessons learned would be appreciated. If there’s no official solution yet, I’d also be interested in whether this is worth posting to the SAP Influence.

items.title: EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD BAdI Implementation for GET_VARIABLE_KEY
items.author: marcel_schaefer
items.text:
The following blog post is relevant only for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Please note that Developer Extensibility is required. 

 Below some example use cases for BAdI EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD~GET_VARIABLE_KEY 
 Chile: Modification of the standard determination of DTE type 
 Colombia: Use BAdI to change the variable key used for selection of customizing activity "Assign Number Ranges to eDocument Types" 
 Peru: Use BAdI to change the variable key used for selection of customizing activity "Assign Series and Number Range to Document Type" 

 Implementation 
 To implement, use method "if_edoc_adaptor_cloud~get_variable_key" in BAdI EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD (enhancement spot ES_EDOCUMENT_CLOUD). The method “get_variable_key” receives the source data in the importing parameter “is_source_data”, "iv_source_key", "iv_source_type" and "iv_edoc_type". The changing parameter “ cv_varkey ” allows you to change the variable key. 
 Implementation Steps: 
 Create implementation for enhancement spot ES_DOCUMENT_CLOUD. 
 Create BAdI implementation for EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD. 
 (Optional) Create BAdI Filter for Country and/or Generic Filter. 
 Create implementing class for BAdI EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD, which implements the interfaces "if_badi_interfaces" and "if_edoc_adaptor_cloud". 
 Implement method "get_variable_key" of interface "if_edoc_adaptor_cloud" in your BAdI class. 
 Activate your BAdI implementation.

SAP Sales & Service Cloud Version 2 (SSC V2) , combined with Enterprise Service Management (ESM) , brings a powerful capability to the table: Spatial Services . This feature goes beyond basic CRM functionality — it embeds geospatial intelligence directly into your business processes, starting with one of the most foundational data quality challenges: address validation . 
 This blog explores what Spatial Services are, how they work within SSC V2 and ESM, and why address validation during Account creation is not just a technical nicety but a critical business enabler. 

 What Are Spatial Services? 
 Spatial Services in SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 provide geospatial capabilities that enrich your business data with location intelligence. At their core, they allow your system to: 
 Validate postal addresses against authoritative geospatial data sources 
 Notify users in real time whether an address is verified or unverified 
 Integrate with mapping and data quality platforms such as HERE Maps and SAP Data Quality Management (SAP DQM) 
 Think of Spatial Services as the geospatial backbone that ensures the data your sales and service teams work with is accurate, complete, and trusted from the moment it enters the system. 
 The Business Case: Address Validation for Account Creation 
 Why Address Quality Matters 
 When a sales representative creates a new Account — whether it's a corporate customer, a partner, or an individual customer — the address they enter becomes the foundation for: 
 Business Process Impact of Bad Address Data 
 Sales territory management Incorrect assignments, missed opportunities 
 Order-to-cash and invoicing Failed deliveries, billing disputes 
 Field service dispatching Wasted technician time, SLA breaches 
 Marketing campaigns Undeliverable communications, compliance risks 
 Compliance & KYC Regulatory failures, audit exposure 
 A single incorrectly entered address can cascade across multiple downstream processes — creating operational friction, customer dissatisfaction, and avoidable costs. 
 How Spatial Services Solve This 
 When Address Validation is enabled in SAP SSC V2 Spatial Services, the moment a user creates or updates an Account, the system: 
 Captures the address entered in the Account form 
 Calls the validation engine — either HERE Maps (native integration) or SAP Data Quality Management (if integrated) — to verify the address against real-world geospatial data 
 Returns a validation status — clearly marking the address as Verified or Not Verified directly on the record 
 Notifies the user so they can correct the address on the spot, before bad data propagates into the system 
 This real-time feedback loop transforms address entry from a passive text field into an active data quality gate . 
 Real-World Business Use Case Walkthrough 
 Scenario: Onboarding a New B2B Account 
 Without Spatial Services: 
 A sales rep types "123 Elm Streeet, Chciago, IL 60601" — two typos, unnoticed. The record is saved. Two weeks later, a product sample shipment fails, a service technician is dispatched to the wrong location, and the territory manager's reporting is skewed. 
 With Spatial Services + Address Validation enabled: 
 The same rep enters the address. SSC V2 immediately validates it against HERE Maps. A "Not Verified" indicator appears with a suggestion: "Did you mean 123 Elm Street, Chicago, IL 60601?" The rep corrects it in seconds. The record is saved clean. 
 The value is immediate, measurable, and permanent — every Account created from that point forward carries trusted address data. 
 Under the Hood: Two Validation Paths 
 SAP SSC V2 Spatial Services support two validation modes depending on your landscape: 
 1. HERE Maps (Default) 
 When Address Validation is turned on without a DQM integration, HERE Maps is used as the geospatial validation engine. HERE Maps is a globally recognised mapping platform with comprehensive coverage of postal addresses worldwide — making it ideal for multinational sales and service operations. 

 2. SAP Data Quality Management (SAP DQM) 
 If your organization has integrated SSC V2 with SAP Data Quality Management , DQM takes over as the validation engine. SAP DQM offers enterprise-grade address cleansing, standardization, and enrichment — particularly valuable for organizations with: 
 High-volume account creation workflows 
 Complex regulatory compliance requirements 
 Existing SAP MDG (Master Data Governance) landscapes 
 This dual-path architecture gives organizations the flexibility to start with HERE Maps and graduate to SAP DQM as their data governance maturity increases. 
 Configuration: Getting Spatial Services Running 
 Setting up Spatial Services in SSC V2 is straightforward and follows a standard administrator workflow. 
 Step 1 — Configure Users and Access Control 
 As an administrator, you need to grant the right people access to Spatial Services: 
 Create a Business Role for users who will work with or administer Spatial Services 
 Add the Business Service : sap.crm.spatialservice.uiapp.spatial 
 Enable the Admin App : sap.crm.spatialservice.uiapp.spatialAdmin (service: sap.crm.service.spatialService ) 
 This role-based approach ensures that spatial capabilities are available to the right personas — whether it's a sales operations admin or a data steward — without over-provisioning access. 
 Step 2 — Enable Address Validation in General Settings 
 Navigate to: 
 User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Spatial Services → General 

 Turn on the Address Validation switch. Once enabled: 
 Address validation is active for Accounts and Individual Customers 
 HERE Maps begins validating addresses immediately (or SAP DQM, if integrated) 
 The verification status indicator appears on the relevant entity forms 
 New Account Creation - Validate Address 
 Existing Account - Validate Address 
 I ndividual Customer - Validate Address 
 Visits - Validate Address and Here Map 
 Key Benefits for Sales & Service Operations 
 Benefit Detail 
 Higher CRM data quality Addresses are validated at source, not cleaned up later 
 Better territory management Accurate geocoding supports precise sales territory assignments 
 Faster field service dispatch Technicians are routed to real, verified locations 
 Reduced invoice and delivery errors Clean addresses mean fewer order and shipment failures 
 Lower data remediation costs Prevention is cheaper than correction — always 
 Compliance readiness Verified customer addresses support KYC and regulatory requirements 
 ESM Perspective: Spatial Services in Service Management 
 From an Enterprise Service Management standpoint, address validation plays an equally critical role. When service tickets, maintenance plans, or on-site work orders are tied to an Account or Installation Point, the underlying address accuracy directly affects: 
 Service Level Agreement (SLA) adherence — routing delays from bad addresses cause SLA breaches 
 Resource scheduling — field service scheduling engines (like SAP Field Service Management) depend on precise geocoordinates derived from validated addresses 
 Customer experience — a technician arriving at the right place, on time, is the most direct signal of service quality to your customer 
 Spatial Services bridges the gap between CRM data entry and operational service execution — making it a shared capability that both Sales and Service teams depend on. 
 What's Next: Growing with Spatial Services 
 Address validation is the first and most impactful use case, but Spatial Services is designed to grow. As SAP SSC V2 evolves, expect spatial capabilities to extend into: 
 Map-based account and opportunity visualization — see your pipeline on a map 
 Geo-fencing for territory management — dynamically assign accounts based on boundaries 
 Location-aware service routing — optimize field service dispatch using real-time geo data 
 Proximity-based lead scoring — score leads by their proximity to existing high-value accounts 
 Conclusion 
 SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2's Spatial Services — and specifically its address validation capability — is a deceptively simple feature with outsized business impact. By catching bad address data at the point of Account creation, organizations protect the integrity of every downstream process that depends on it: shipping, invoicing, field service, territory management, and compliance. 
 For SAP customers running SSC V2 with ESM, enabling Address Validation via HERE Maps or SAP DQM is one of the highest-ROI configuration steps an administrator can take. It costs minutes to configure and delivers data quality dividends for the entire lifecycle of every Account record in your system. 
 Clean data in. Better business outcomes out. That's the promise of Spatial Services. 
 Have questions about configuring Spatial Services in your SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 landscape? Feel free to reach out or drop a comment below.

items.title: Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation
items.author: felixbartler
items.text:
Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation 
 In a previous post we looked at connecting a custom A2A agent to S/4HANA Public Cloud with full principal propagation. But that approach comes with some drawbacks: hooking up individual APIs doesn't scale well, and it's hard to enforce governance. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for exposing tools and data to AI agents in a uniform way, and it's quickly becoming the common language between agents and enterprise systems. SAP's reference architecture for Agents and MCP positions Integration Suite as an MCP Gateway to safeguard traffic to enterprise systems — so this post extends the example to route a BTP-based agent through that gateway, still from customer-managed Joule. 
 Note: This post covers Customer-Managed Joule. 
 Scenario 
 We have an A2A-capable agent connected to Joule (customer-managed), with a destination that hands the Joule user's token to the agent on each A2A request. To reach S/4HANA Public Cloud, that agent now goes through the MCP Gateway : Integration Suite points its gateway at an S/4HANA OData service via a destination, the selected endpoints become MCP tools, and it all runs on Integration Cell. The user identity is propagated the whole way — from Joule, through the custom agent, through the MCP Gateway, into S/4HANA — so the backend call runs as the real user. And because the gateway sits on Integration Suite, we inherit the API Management controls we already know: additional authentication and authorization on top, plus IP filtering, rate limiting and quotas where we need them. 
 This matters because many customers have built their agents in an A2A manner, and their API policy often restricts them to endorsed architectures only. 

 Prerequisites 
 A working A2A agent and destination setup, as described in the principal propagation post 
 An S/4HANA Public Cloud system 
 Integration Suite, Premium Edition (only that Edition contains the MCP Gateway) 
 Step 1: Trust the Integration Suite subaccount in S/4 
 The very first step diverges from the previous post: the trust setup . Last time we configured S/4 to trust the destination certificate of the agent's subaccount. This time the piece that resolves the SAML Bearer assertion is the destination service of the subaccount where Integration Suite lives — and that is a different subaccount, with a different signing certificate (at least in my case). So we repeat the communication setup against that subaccount. 
 Concretely, in your Integration Suite subaccount go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust and grab the .pem . It is a self-signed cert whose subject looks like cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/<subaccount-id> with OU=CP Destination Configuration — this is the destination-service signing certificate. 
 Then, exactly as in the principal propagation post , set up a communication user, a communication system and a communication arrangement ( SAP_COM_0008 for Business Partner) in S/4 — but upload this certificate under the communication system's OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider , and copy its subject CN into the Provider Name field. 
 Note: if the trust is missing or points at the wrong subaccount, the SAML exchange later fails with a very explicit "There is no trust between entities … in client 100" . That message contains the subaccount ID it actually saw, which makes it easy to tell that you trusted the wrong one. 
 Step 2: Create the S/4HANA SAML Bearer destination in the IS subaccount 
 Next, create an HTTP destination toward S/4HANA in the subaccount where Integration Suite resides . This is the same OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion destination as in the previous post — the MCP server will use it as its target. The important properties: Name=S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap
Audience=https://my3xxxxx.s4hana.cloud.sap
Token Service URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/bc/sec/oauth2/token
Client Key / Token Service User=<the comm user from step 1>
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:X509
userIdSource=mail
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

# additional properties
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs
IntegrationCell.Include=true 
 Two things that are easy to miss: 
 x_user_token.jwks_uri points at the IAS tenant so the destination service can validate the forwarded end-user token and build the SAML assertion for the real user. Without it, it silently falls back to a technical-user assertion and propagation breaks. 
 IntegrationCell.Include=true is a label on the destination. Without it the destination simply won't appear in the MCP Server wizard's dropdown at all. 
 Step 3: Build the MCP server in Integration Suite 
 Now the new part. In Design → Integrations and APIs , create an integration package to hold the artifact. 

 Inside the package, add an MCP Server artifact. The wizard's first step asks for the source type — pick HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification : 

 In the next step, point it at the S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST destination with a relative URL of /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER , give it a name and an MCP Path (e.g. /s4_bp_mcp ), and leave the runtime profile on Integration Cell : 

 Skip the AI spec generation. Once the artifact exists, open its MCP Configuration → Source tab and hit Edit API Specification to supply the spec: 

 Import the OpenAPI/EDMX of the Business Partner service — you can download it from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub , or just pull the live $metadata from your own system: 

 On the Tools tab, select the operations you want to expose; each one becomes an MCP tool. I started with a single GET A_BusinessPartner → the tool get_A_BusinessPartner . Keep it small; the model routes better with fewer, well-described tools: 

 The tricky part is the inbound security — this is where the whole principal-propagation story lives. On the Policies tab every MCP server has a mandatory Authentication and Authorization policy, so we look at both. 
 Authentication 
 The Authentication policy decides which tokens the gateway trusts . By default an MCP server validates tokens issued through the Integration Suite subaccount's own XSUAA / the IdP configured there. That default path is enough for a client like Joule Work Desktop , which runs its own user-token fetch flow against that trusted authorization server when you add the connector — so the end-user identity is already there, you don't configure anything extra on the gateway. 
 Our case is different: the token doesn't come from a JWD connector, it's the JWT our A2A agent forwards from Joule, issued by our IAS tenant — and a raw token from that issuer is rejected by the default policy with 401 invalidToken because the gateway doesn't trust it yet. 
 The fix is to switch the Authentication policy to External OAuth (OIDC) and point it at our IAS tenant. Even though this feels a bit strange — our IAS tenant is treated as an "external" OAuth provider here — the "internal" option is the subaccount's XSUAA, which may well itself be configured to redirect logins to exactly that same IAS. So "external" just means: validate the token directly against the IAS tenant, by its own issuer and keys. 

 Once External OAuth is selected, there are four fields to fill: 
 Field Value 
 Well-Known URL https://<ias-tenant>/.well-known/openid-configuration 
 Audience the aud of the token the client actually sends (see the gotcha below) 
 ClientID Key ${authn.oidc.jwt.azp} 
 UserInfo Key ${authn.oidc.jwt.mail} 
 What these actually do: the Well-Known URL tells the gateway which IAS tenant to trust — it discovers the issuer and the signing keys from there, and validates every incoming token's signature against them. The Audience is the gateway saying "I only accept tokens that were actually meant for this application" — it's matched against the token's aud claim. ClientID Key and UserInfo Key are expressions that tell the gateway which claims carry the calling client's ID ( azp ) and the end user's identity ( mail ) — the latter being exactly the identity that gets propagated downstream. 
 The Audience is the one that'll bite you. Our destination maps userIdSource=mail , and the token that eventually arrives is the one Joule forwarded — i.e. after its app-to-app exchange — so its aud is the Custom Agent App client ID, not the login app you used to get a test token. You find that client ID in your IAS admin console under Applications → your Custom Agent App → Client ID (it's the same value that your agent already validates as its IAS_AUDIENCE ). If you set the policy audience to the wrong app, the real Joule token is rejected with 401 invalidToken even though everything else is correct. You can also list multiple audiences comma-separated, or leave it empty to skip audience validation entirely while debugging. 
 If authentication is not configured correctly, the gateway rejects the call before it ever reaches your backend — a decoded IAS token that doesn't match issuer/audience comes back as: { "error": { "code": "invalidToken", "message": "Unable to authenticate user, invalid token" } } 
 (HTTP 401) 
 Authorization 
 The second mandatory policy is Authorization — and this is where it helps to understand how an IAS token is built, because it is fundamentally different from the XSUAA token you may be used to. 
 An XSUAA access token carries a scope claim (things like myapp.Read , API.invoke ), and the default Authorization policy checks exactly that: does the token contain the required scope? An IAS token has no scope claim at all. IAS is an identity provider — it answers "who are you", not "what may you do"; the actual authorization is expected to happen in the target system (the user's S/4 roles, in our case). A decoded IAS user token has mail , sub , azp — but nothing a scope-based policy can match on. 
 What an IAS token does carry, because it came through Joule's app-to-app exchange, is the ias_apis claim — a list of the exposed APIs the user is allowed to call: {
 "iss": "https://<ias-tenant>",
 "aud": "<custom-agent-app client id>",
 "azp": "<proxy-app client id>",
 "mail": "felix.bartler@sap.com",
 "ias_apis": ["a2a_custom_agent_app_api"]
} 
 So the configuration change versus the XSUAA default is: don't check a scope claim, check the ias_apis list instead. Point the Authorization policy's Scope Key at ias_apis and set the expected value to our exposed API: 
 Authorization field Value 
 Authorization Type OAuth Scope OR Developer Key 
 Scope Key ias_apis 
 Scope a2a_custom_agent_app_api 
 The policy then checks whether the ias_apis list contains a2a_custom_agent_app_api — which doubles as a useful access gate: it enforces, right at the gateway, that only users entitled to this agent's exposed API can call it at all. 

 If authorization is wrong — e.g. the policy still checks scope , which an IAS token doesn't have — the gateway authenticates the user fine but then refuses the operation: { "error": { "code": "forbidden", "message": "User doesn't have the authorization to perform this operation" } } 
 (HTTP 403) 
 With both policies right, the gateway accepts the real Joule user token, validates it against IAS, reads mail , and forwards the identity to the destination. 
 Deploy MCP Server 
 Finally Deploy onto the Integration Cell runtime, and once the Runtime Status reads STARTED the MCP URL is live: 

 We've basically turned an OData endpoint into a proper MCP Server — with a curated list of tools — and put an auth layer in front of it that enforces principal propagation. Let's test it: 
 Testing the gateway with curl

items.title: Using OAuth2 Client Credentials to access REST APIs in SAP Sales/Service Cloud Version 2
items.author: Felix_Wyskocil
items.text:
Introduction 
 While Communication System -based integration in SAP Sales/Service Cloud Version 2 (for instance with SAP S/4HANA ) relies on Basic Authentication or X.509 client certificates for inbound connections, you can use OAuth 2.0 with the Client Credentials grant type for accessing the REST APIs in machine-to-machine scenarios without setting up a communication system. Only a technical user needs to be created. 
 In this blog, I'll show you how to set up OAuth2 Client Credentials and configure them in two sample clients. 

 Why OAuth2 Client Credentials? 
 A high-level comparison with the previously mentioned methods: 
 Basic Auth is easy to implement and to use. However, it sends the secret (the password) "unencrypted" to the API endpoint, usually with every call. As long as HTTPS is in use, the connection itself is encrypted at the transport layer. However, if an attacker manages to eavesdrop on the connection (e.g., man-in-the-middle attack), the secret is known and could thus be used for unauthorized access to the target system. For that reason, you should only use it for testing purposes in test environments. 
 X.509 Client Certificates offer strong mutual authentication where the secret (in this case the private key) is never transmitted to the recipient. Instead, cryptographic computations on data that changes with every session prove the identity of the server and the client. B ut this comes with significant operational overhead: certificate issuance, rotation, revocation, and trust store management across every consumer. 
 OAuth2 shifts the model: Credentials are exchanged once at a dedicated authorization server, and the resulting short-lived access token is what travels across APIs. That means the s ecret never reaches the resource server (compared to Basic Auth). 
 Tokens carry embedded scope and expiry information, and are usually signed (depending on the validation method), which limits the impact if intercepted. Signing and validating tokens happens "behind the scenes" for the caller and keeps this complexity away from them. 
 The Client Credentials flow is OAuth2 stripped down for machine-to-machine communication: No user context, no browser redirect. Just a system identity authenticating against an authorization server and calling the actual API at the resource server . 

 Setting Up OAuth2 Client Credentials for REST APIs in SAP Sales/Service Cloud Version 2 
 1. Create a Technical Role for the API user 
 If you don't already have a technical role with all required permissions, create a new one: 
 Go to User Menu --> System Settings --> (Users and Control) --> Roles --> switch the view from Business Roles to Technical Roles 

 Assign the services that the API user(s), who get this role assigned later, need. You can assign this role to multiple technical users. 
 Don't forget to Active the role. 

 2. Create Technical User and assign the Technical Role 
 Go to User Menu --> System Settings --> (Users and Control) --> Users --> switch the view from Business Users to Technical Users 

 Create a new technical user using the [+] button. (In contrast to business users, technical users can be created without an employee.) 
 You don't need to assign a password or upload a certificate for this user. The OAuth settings will be maintained on a different screen. Also, the entered user name will not be used outside of the system. It is just for your reference/to identify it. 
 Assign the technical role and save the technical user. 

 3. Open the technical user and Generate Client Credentials 
 A dialog will be displayed that lets you copy the clientid and the clientsecret . 
 Please note that the clientsecret will only be displayed once! (see next step) 

 After initially generating the Client Credentials, you can only view the clientid . You can't view the clientsecret . If you forget the clientsecret, you can only generate a new clientsecret . 

 After these steps, you can configure clients to use OAuth 2 with the Client Credentials grant type to access SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2's REST APIs. Pay attention to additional properties that OAuth2 requires for handing over tokens, etc. I'll mention two examples for common clients in the next section. 

 Configuring Clients 
 Bruno API Client 
 In Bruno, you can set up OAuth 2.0 with the Client Credentials Grant Type on the Auth tab, either for a single request, or for a folder or collection, which allows you to inherit this Auth method to all requests in that folder or collection. 
 The following screenshot shows the most relevant elements of the Auth tab maintained for a single request that fetches the first 3 accounts from the system. 
 Maintain the following configuration attributes: 
 Access Token URL : https://<<SSCV2_HOST>>/oauth/token 
 Client ID : <<your client id>> 
 Client Secret : <<your client secret>> 
 Add Credentials to : Basic Auth Header 
 For the Token attributes, I could use the Bruno defaults: 
 Token Source : Access Token 
 Token ID : credentials 
 Add token to : Headers 
 Header Prefix : Bearer 

 After you've maintained all the authentication details, you can click Get Access Token or directly send the request, which fetches the access token on demand. 

 SAP Integration Suite / Cloud Integration 
 The second example demonstrates how to call SAP Sales/Service Cloud v2's Accounts REST API (the same service as above in Bruno) from an integration flow (iFlow) in SAP Integration Suite/Cloud Integration using OAuth2 Client Credentials. This requires two steps: 
 Create a Security Material 
 Use the Security Material in an iFlow 
 1. Create the Security Material 
 In SAP Integration Suite, go to Monitor --> Integrations and APIs --> (Manage Security) --> Security Material 
 If you don't see the Create button on this screen, make sure the Runtime filter is set to All . 
 Choose Create --> OAuth2 Client Credentials and maintain the following attributes: 
 Name : <<credential name as later used in the iflow>> 
 Token Service URL : https://<<SSCV2_HOST>>/oauth/token 
 Grant Type : Send as Part of Body 
 Client ID : <<your client id>> 
 Client Secret : <<your client secret>> 
 Client Authentication : Send as Request Header 
 Content Type : application/x-www-form-urlencoded 
 The following screenshot shows the Manage Security Material screen. Make sure to adapt the default values of the highlighted fields. 

 After you have deployed the security material, you can use it in the iFlow. 

 2. Design the Integration Flow 
 The sample iFlow only consists of a single HTTP Request-Reply call to the Accounts REST API using the previously created security material. That means, the sample iFlow returns the first 3 accounts from SSCv2 as a JSON body to the iFlow caller. 
 The important properties can be found in the Connection tab: 
 Authentication must be set to OAuth2 Client Credentials 
 Credential Name must be set to the name of the previously created security material 
 (in the sample screenshot below, the name is parameterized to allow users to configure it without editing the iFlow) 

 I hope this blog was helpful for getting started with OAuth2 Client Credentials in SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2.

items.title: From Nonconformances to Action: Connecting n8n, AI, and SAP Digital Manufacturing
items.author: ManoelCosta
items.text:
Introduction 
 After my first hands-on experiment with n8n and SAP Digital Manufacturing, where I retrieved manufacturing alerts and used an AI Agent to summarize and prioritize them, I decided to take the next step. 
 This time, I wanted to explore a manufacturing quality scenario: how can we use AI to analyze open nonconformances, provide actionable recommendations to production supervisors, and automatically raise alerts for critical issues directly in SAP Digital Manufacturing? 
 The idea is simple. Manufacturing systems already capture valuable information about production issues, but identifying the right priorities and deciding what to do next can require time and manual effort. 
 By combining SAP Digital Manufacturing, n8n, and a Large Language Model (LLM), we can build a workflow that transforms nonconformance data into actionable insights and connects critical findings back to the manufacturing system. 
 Let's explore how it works!

items.title: Introducing new 'Monitor Alerts' application in SAP Asset Performance Management
items.author: Young-Hoe_Koo
items.text:
Alex starts every shift the same way. Open Monitor Alerts, scan the queue, figure out what needs attention. On a quiet day that takes ten minutes. On a bad day, it takes all morning - not because the alerts are complex, but because getting the full picture means bouncing between applications, chasing down who looked at something last, and eventually giving up and just starting from scratch. 
 Alert management sounds simple in theory. An indicator breaches a threshold, an alert is raised, someone investigates, and maintenance action follows. In practice, it is rarely that clean. 
 The alert exists, but who owns it? What happened before it was raised? Has anyone already acted on it? Where is the full picture of this asset's health? The old Monitor Alerts application gave you the alert. Getting answers to those questions meant going elsewhere. 
 In release 2610, SAP Asset Performance Management introduces a significantly improved Monitor Alerts experience - rebuilt on the SAP Cloud Application Programming (CAP) framework. That is not just a technical detail. CAP is what makes the application extensible, structured, and ready to grow with your process. And it is what enables the new capabilities that ship alongside it. 
 A complete workflow, in one place 
 Start with context 
 Alex g lances at the Monitor Alerts tile on his Fiori launchpad to see how many brand new alerts are waiting. Today there are 19 new alerts waiting. 
 SAP APM Fiori launchpad showing the new Monitor Alerts tile with 19 alerts highlighted in the Asset Health Monitoring section, alongside the legacy application. 
 A VIBRATION_SURGE alert has landed in Alex's queue. A centrifugal pump has a sudden spike in vibration, and this is not the first time. Before deciding anything, Alex needs to know whether this is a recurring pattern or an isolated event - and what the pump's broader health looks like right now. 
 The new Monitor Alerts application answers that without making you leave it. The Indicator Monitoring tab now includes an Additional Information section with a direct link to the Explore Technical Objects application. One click opens all associated alerts and the full indicator chart for that technical object, in a new tab. You stay in context. You get the data you need to make a call. 
 Monitor Alerts detail view for a Vibration Surge alert, showing the Indicator Monitoring tab with the Additional Information section — selecting the Centrifugal Pump 1 CM link opens the Explore Technical Objects application. 
 For more information, see Viewing Alerts 
 Put someone in charge 
 Alex investigates and it is clear this one needs a closer look - but Alex is heading into a planning meeting in twenty minutes. Someone else needs to pick it up. 
 The new Assigned To field lets you designate a processor for each alert directly in Monitor Alerts. Everyone on the team can see who is handling what, which means less duplication and fewer things falling through the gaps. 
 Vibration Surge alert in edit mode, showing the Administrative Information section with the Assigned To field highlighted, where you can enter the responsible processor. 
 The alert does not sit in a shared queue waiting for someone to claim it. It has an owner. 
 For more information, see Assigning a Processor to an Alert . 
 Know exactly what happened 
 Later that day, a colleague asks about the same pump unit. Alex pulls up the alert and everything is there - who looked at it, when the status changed, what follow-up was linked. 
 Every change to an alert is now recorded in a dedicated Change Log tab. Status updates, reassignments, linked follow-up actions - all of it is captured automatically. If you need to understand what happened to an alert and when, the answer is right there. 
 Vibration Surge alert Change Log tab showing two entries - a notification created with number 12851897 and a status update from New to In Process - recording who made each change and when 
 For more information, see Alert Change Log . 
 Turn insights into action without switching systems 
 The pattern is confirmed. This pump needs a maintenance notification. Alex used to have to open S/4HANA separately, find the right equipment record, and create the notification from scratch. 
 Now you can create a Maintenance Notification in SAP S/4HANA directly from Monitor Alerts. And when you do, you can optionally set a Detection Method - a field that captures how the failure was discovered. Was it flagged during a planned inspection? Picked up by condition monitoring? That information feeds back into failure analysis and helps teams improve how they detect and respond over time. 

 For more information, see Create Notification . 
 He can also now navigate directly from Monitor Alerts to the corresponding S/4HANA Maintenance Notification. No switching between systems manually, and no searching for the right record. 

 Built to be extended 
 Alex works in a large industrial operation with workflows and terminology that do not map perfectly to any out-of-the-box application. That used to mean workarounds. 
 Because Monitor Alerts is built on CAP, it supports SaaS extensibility. If your organization needs to adapt the application to specific workflows, add custom fields, or integrate with other services, the Cloud Application Programming framework gives you the foundation to do that in a structured, upgrade-safe way. 
 For more information, see Extending Multi-Service Applications . 
 To sum up 
 By the time Alex closes out for the day, the queue looks different. Alerts have owners. The change log shows exactly what happened and when. A maintenance notification is already in S/4HANA. And nothing fell through the cracks. 
 Better navigation. Clear ownership. Full traceability. Direct integration with SAP S/4HANA. And a foundation built for the future.
